cards.q: Why does the Labor Movement matter?
cards.a: The labor movement turned the problems of industrial work into public questions. Its defeats in the Gilded Age and its victory in the New Deal shaped the rights that American workers have today.

Industrial workers toiled long hours for little pay. A typical industrial laborer, the American Yawp notes, worked sixty hours a week, could expect to be out of work one month a year, and might still earn less than a poverty-line income.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: The Great Upheaval of 1877. In 1877, in the stagnant economy that followed the collapse of the railroad bubble in 1873, rail lines slashed wages.

cards.q: Why does the Chinese Exclusion Act matter?
cards.a: The act made race and nationality explicit grounds for excluding immigrants. The Geary Act of 1892 added a requirement that every Chinese resident register and carry a certificate of residence or face deportation.

Chinese immigrants, mostly from Guangdong Province, came to California from the 1850s, driven by famine, rebellion, and economic collapse at home. Welcomed at first as laborers in the gold fields and on the railroads, they became scapegoats when the economy faltered in the 1870s.

Exclusion of laborers. Chinese laborers, defined as “skilled and unskilled… and Chinese employed in mining,” were barred for ten years. Narrow exceptions. Merchants, diplomats, students, and other non-laborers could enter only with certification from the Chinese government — difficult to obtain in practice. No naturalization. Federal and state courts were forbidden to grant citizenship to Chinese immigrants, who could still be deported. Re-entry certificates. Chinese residents who left the country needed certificates to return.

cards.q: Why does Statue of Liberty matter?
cards.a: The Statue of Liberty is perhaps the best-known symbol of the United States — a monument to independence and the end of slavery that came to stand above all for the promise America offered immigrants.

The statue stands on Liberty Island (formerly Bedloe’s Island) in New York Harbor, on a pedestal set within Fort Wood, an 11-point Army fort built in the early 1800s. Lady Liberty holds a torch in her right hand and, in her left, a tablet inscribed with the date of the Declaration of Independence.

In 1865 the French historian and abolitionist Édouard de Laboulaye proposed a monumental gift from the people of France to the people of the United States — to mark the centennial of American independence and to celebrate the recent abolition of slavery. Sculptor Bartholdi took up the idea.

cards.a: Haymarket became a symbol of the bitter conflict between labor and capital in the Gilded Age — and of how fear of radicalism could override due process.

cards.a: On May 3, police fired on strikers at the McCormick Harvesting Machine Company, leaving one man dead and many injured. Labor activists called a protest rally for the next evening.
On May 4 at 7:30 p.m., around 1,500 people gathered on Desplaines Street near Haymarket Square. Chicago’s mayor, Carter Harrison, attended as an observer and confirmed the meeting was peaceful.

cards.q: Why does the Dawes Act matter?
cards.a: The act’s stated purpose was to protect Native property rights, but the results were very different.
By the 1880s, after the wars on the Plains, most Native nations had been confined to reservations. Federal policy shifted from removal and war to assimilation.

Severalty. Reservation land would be divided among individual tribal members who registered on a tribal roll, rather than held by the nation in common. Assimilation. Lawmakers reasoned that people who adopted “White” clothing and ways and farmed their own land would lose their “Indian-ness” and no longer need government supervision. Exemptions — at first. Section 8 exempted the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Seminole, and several other nations, but later laws and the Dawes Commission (from 1893) extended allotment to them in exchange for abolishing their tribal governments.

cards.q: Why does Populism and the People’s Party matter?
cards.a: The Populist revolt was the largest third-party challenge of the Gilded Age, and it put the regulation of corporations and the expansion of democracy on the national agenda.
Populists believed national policies favored industry, banks, and the Northeast over farmers, who faced falling crop prices, debt, and high railroad rates.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: Farmers organized through cooperative Farmers’ Alliances and then turned to independent politics.

Americans in these years had many different ideas about how the country should develop and whose interests needed the most protection. Reformers wanted to clean up politics, and Black Americans kept up their long fight for civil rights.

cards.a: Exposure. Journalists whom Theodore Roosevelt called “muckrakers” exposed business practices, poverty, and corruption in magazines such as McClure’s. Jacob Riis’s How the Other Half Lives (1890) used photographs to show the city’s slums and led to housing reform.

cards.a: The massacre at Wounded Knee is remembered as the violent end of the Plains wars and as one of the gravest atrocities committed by U.S. forces against Native people.

cards.q: What led to the Wounded Knee Massacre?
cards.a: White settlers and federal officials feared the Ghost Dance meant an armed uprising, and troops were sent to the Lakota reservations. On December 15, 1890, Lakota police trying to arrest Sitting Bull at Standing Rock killed him.
On the morning of December 29, cavalrymen entered the camp to disarm the band. Tensions flared and a shot was fired — it is unclear by whom.

Ellis Island is the gateway through which a large share of today’s Americans trace their ancestry — a symbol of the nation as a land of immigrants, and of the restrictions that ended the era of mass European migration.
Ellis Island sits in New York Harbor near the Statue of Liberty. Arriving immigrants — especially those traveling in steerage — were ferried to the island for medical and legal inspection.

Ellis Island opened as a federal immigration station in 1892, during an era of mass migration. Between 1870 and 1940 more than 25 million immigrants came to the United States, with arrivals peaking at nearly 900,000 a year in the period 1900–1914.

cards.q: Why does the Overthrow and Annexation of Hawaiʻi matter?
cards.a: The annexation of Hawaiʻi marked the United States’ turn toward overseas empire in the Pacific. It was carried out against the will of most Native Hawaiians — after a coup that a U.S. investigation called illegal, and by a joint resolution that bypassed the treaty process.

cards.q: What led to the Overthrow and Annexation of Hawaiʻi?
cards.a: The planters wanted to protect their profits. They feared that the United States would impose a tariff on Hawaiian sugar and wanted to protect the islands’ free-trade status with the United States, their main customer.

On July 6, 1887, a militia tied to the Hawaiian League, a party of mostly American businessmen led by Lorrin Thurston, forced King Kalākaua to sign a constitution that stripped him of power and many Native Hawaiians of their rights — the “Bayonet Constitution.”

The boycott crippled rail traffic nationwide. The General Managers’ Association, representing 24 railroads, hired strikebreakers and worked to turn public opinion against the strikers.

cards.a: Puerto Rico is one of the territories the United States acquired as it became an overseas empire in 1898. Its unresolved status — citizens without full representation — raises lasting questions about democracy, empire, and what it means to be part of the United States.

cards.q: What led to Puerto Rico Under the United States?
cards.a: Victory over Spain left the United States with island colonies and no settled plan for governing them. Many Americans wanted the strategic and commercial advantages of overseas territory; anti-imperialists warned that ruling peoples without their consent betrayed the nation’s founding ideals.

At first the island was ruled by the U.S. military and a presidentially appointed governor. The Foraker Act of 1900 ended military rule and provided a “temporary civil government for Porto Rico,” as Congress then spelled it, but it did not make Puerto Ricans U.S. citizens.

cards.a: The Spanish-American War marked the moment the United States became an overseas empire, raising questions about democracy, race, and power abroad that would shape the twentieth century.
Since the mid-nineteenth century Cubans had tried to win independence from Spain, and a new revolution began in 1895.

cards.q: Why does the Wright Brothers’ First Flight matter?
cards.a: The first flights opened the age of aviation, which within a few decades transformed war, travel, and commerce. The Wrights’ methodical, experimental approach became a model of American ingenuity.

cards.q: What led to the Wright Brothers’ First Flight?
cards.a: The Wrights needed a place with strong, steady winds to give lift and soft sand for safe landings. After searching the East Coast, they chose the remote dunes near Kitty Hawk, on North Carolina’s Outer Banks.

After months of setbacks, the brothers were ready on December 17, 1903. Men from the Kill Devil Hills Lifesaving Station, about a mile away, had been helping them, ferrying visitors and moving equipment; four of the crewmen came to watch.

cards.q: Why does Angel Island Immigration Station matter?
cards.a: Angel Island reveals the exclusionary side of American immigration history — a gateway where race, not merely health or wealth, determined who could enter.

The station stands on Angel Island, the largest island in San Francisco Bay. Immigration officials chose the site for its isolation, believing it would keep detainees from escaping or communicating with relatives in San Francisco.
Chinese immigrants had come to California since the Gold Rush, but after the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 nearly all Chinese labor immigration was barred.

cards.q: Why does the Great Migration matter?
cards.a: The Great Migration was one of the largest internal movements of people in American history, and it reshaped the racial geography, politics, and culture of the entire nation.
Migrants sought better wages, education for their children, the right to vote, and freedom from the daily humiliations and violence of Jim Crow. Many described the move as a second emancipation.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: Migration was a collective act built on networks of family, churches, and Black newspapers that spread word of jobs and conditions in the North.

cards.q: Why does the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire matter?
cards.a: The Triangle fire made the dangers of industrial work a public scandal. It convinced many Americans that government had to regulate the workplace, and it produced the most thorough investigation of working conditions that any state had yet attempted.

cards.q: What led to the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire?
cards.a: Fire inspection and fire precautions in New York were badly inadequate. On the day of the fire, waste bins full of cloth scraps from the day’s work fed the flames and let them spread fast. The owners had often locked exit doors in the past, saying that workers stole materials. At quitting time workers normally left through one exit on the Greene Street side, where every handbag was inspected. The building’s single fire escape led nowhere safe, and the elevator shaft had only one car. Firefighting equipment could not reach a fire so high up.
Near closing time on March 25, 1911, fire broke out in one of the crowded, littered workrooms. Workers on the eighth and tenth floors escaped.

cards.q: Why does World War I matter?
cards.a: World War I made the United States a world power, but the nation’s rejection of the League of Nations signaled a retreat from the international leadership Wilson had envisioned.

As a neutral trading nation, the United States supplied the Allies with munitions and loans. German submarines targeted shipping around Britain; the sinking of the British liner Lusitania in May 1915 killed more than a hundred Americans.

Unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram (1917): brought the United States into the war. The convoy system: American naval escorts helped counter the U-boat threat. The failure of Germany’s 1918 spring offensives and the Allied counteroffensives: made German defeat inevitable.

cards.q: Why does Schenck v. United States matter?

cards.q: Why does the Nineteenth Amendment matter?
cards.a: The Nineteenth Amendment made women’s suffrage national. It was the work of several generations who, in the National Archives’ words, “lectured, wrote, marched, lobbied, and practiced civil disobedience.” Few of the movement’s early leaders lived to see it, and its promise remained incomplete for many women of color.

The organized movement for women’s votes began at the women’s rights convention in Seneca Falls, New York, in 1848, organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott. After the Civil War, the Fifteenth Amendment barred racial discrimination in voting but not discrimination by sex, which split the suffrage movement into rival associations. In 1878 a woman suffrage amendment was introduced in Congress, beginning a campaign for passage that lasted more than four decades. The two main organizations merged in 1890 as the National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA).
The amendment is two sentences long. Section 1 reads: “The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex.”

cards.q: Why does Tulsa Race Massacre matter?
cards.a: The Tulsa massacre showed how white violence could destroy Black prosperity, and the long silence that followed it shows how communities and nations choose what to remember.

cards.q: What led to Tulsa Race Massacre?
cards.a: On May 30, 1921, an encounter in a downtown elevator between Dick Rowland, a young Black shoe shiner, and Sarah Page, a white elevator operator, set events in motion; the most common explanation is that he stepped on her foot and she screamed.

By evening hundreds of whites had gathered at the county courthouse demanding Rowland. Armed Black men, many of them World War I veterans, twice went to the courthouse to help protect him and were turned away by the sheriff.

cards.q: Why does the Harlem Renaissance matter?
cards.a: The Harlem Renaissance made Black writers, artists, and musicians central to American culture and gave later civil rights generations a powerful tradition of self-expression.

Black Americans entered the 1920s weighed down by Jim Crow segregation, lynching, and the racial violence of 1919’s “Red Summer.” Harlem Renaissance writers and artists sought to define Black life on their own terms.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: The movement worked through culture: novels, poetry, short stories, theater, painting, and music. Locke’s anthology The New Negro (1925) gathered writing by men and women, young and old, Black and white — a book, as The American Yawp puts it, of African Americans rather than only about them.

cards.q: Why does Immigration Act of 1924 matter?
cards.a: The 1924 act wrote ideas about racial and national hierarchy into federal law and sharply curtailed immigration from southern and eastern Europe and Asia.

In 1917, amid wartime anxiety about national security, Congress passed the first broadly restrictive immigration law. It required a literacy test for immigrants over 16 and barred people from an “Asiatic Barred Zone.”

The 1924 law lowered the quota from 3 to 2 percent and moved the base year back from 1910 to 1890 — before the largest waves of immigration from Italy, Poland, Russia, and other parts of southern and eastern Europe.

Route 66 is the classic American road: a record of migration, war, and the automobile’s remaking of everyday life, and a lasting symbol of freedom and the open road.

Route 66 crossed the heart of the country from Chicago to Santa Monica on the Pacific. Along it grew the hotels, filling stations, and restaurants of the automobile age; more than 250 of its buildings, bridges, and road alignments are now listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

The highway was created in 1926 to serve the rising number of cars. During the 1930s it carried emigrants out of the Dust Bowl — westward migrants disparagingly called “Okies” by their new neighbors, whose plight John Steinbeck captured in The Grapes of Wrath (1939).

Mount Rushmore is both a celebration of American democracy and a reminder of broken treaties — one of the clearest places to see how a single monument can carry opposite meanings.
The memorial sits on a granite face of the Black Hills, the easternmost extension of the Rocky Mountains, in Pennington County, South Dakota.

The name Black Hills comes from the Lakota Paha Sapa, “hills of black.” By the late 1700s the Lakota controlled the region after defeating the Cheyenne, and religious ceremonies were held there every year.

cards.q: Why does Stock Market Crash of 1929 matter?
cards.a: The Crash of 1929 became the symbolic beginning of the Great Depression and a lasting warning about speculation and borrowed money.

cards.q: What led to Stock Market Crash of 1929?
cards.a: Federal Reserve officials believed speculation was diverting credit from productive uses. The Board urged reserve banks to deny credit to member banks that lent to speculators, and in August 1929 it allowed the New York Fed to raise its discount rate to 6 percent.

Prices peaked on September 3, 1929. As they fell in October, leading bankers met at the offices of J. P. Morgan, pooled funds, and publicly bought blocks of shares at high prices to restore confidence.

cards.q: Why does the Great Depression matter?
cards.a: The Great Depression was the worst economic disaster in American history. It discredited the belief that the economy would right itself without government help and gave rise to the New Deal and the modern federal government.

cards.q: What led to the Great Depression?
cards.a: Historians and economists still debate the Depression’s causes, and most see several working together. The Miller Center lists structural weaknesses in agriculture and industry, a fragile international economy, and a speculative, unstable financial sector, all of which created a badly unequal distribution of wealth: “a consumer economy in which few consumed.”
The crash. On Thursday, October 24, 1929, stock prices suddenly plunged.

cards.q: Why does the Dust Bowl matter?
cards.a: The Dust Bowl was one of the worst environmental disasters in American history, a human-made catastrophe as much as a natural one, and it changed how Americans farm and manage land.

cards.q: What led to the Dust Bowl?
cards.a: Drought covered almost the entire Plains for nearly a decade, in at least four distinct episodes that came too quickly for the land to recover. With the ground cover gone and few windbreaks, high winds churned the dry topsoil into storms that people called “black blizzards” or “dusters.”
Dust storms blotted out the sun, choked people and livestock,. Some carried dirt as far east as Washington, D.C., New England, and ships on the Atlantic.

cards.q: Why does Bonnie and Clyde matter?
cards.a: Bonnie and Clyde show how Americans turned real Depression-era violence into romantic legend — and how popular culture, especially film, can reshape the memory of history.

cards.q: What led to Bonnie and Clyde?
cards.a: Parker met Barrow in January 1930, shortly before he was jailed. She smuggled a pistol into his cell, which he used to escape; he was recaptured in Middletown, Ohio, and sentenced to fourteen years at hard labor.

cards.q: Why does the New Deal matter?
cards.a: The New Deal did not end the Great Depression, but it made the federal government responsible for the economic security of ordinary Americans. It created institutions, from Social Security to the FDIC, that still shape American life.

cards.q: What led to the New Deal?
cards.a: The New Deal had no single blueprint.

The Hundred Days. “The only thing we have to fear is fear itself,” Roosevelt said in his inaugural address. Two days later he declared a national bank holiday, and Congress passed his Emergency Banking Act almost sight unseen.

cards.q: Why does Social Security Act matter?
cards.a: The Social Security Act established that the federal government shares responsibility for Americans’ economic security in old age and hard times. Expanded many times since, it became the centerpiece of the American social welfare state.

Before the 1930s, caring for the elderly was left to families, localities, and states; except for veterans’ pensions, Washington played no role. The Great Depression wiped out savings and jobs and built support for national old-age insurance.

Unlike many European systems, American old-age insurance was funded by “contributions” — taxes on individual wages and employer payrolls — rather than general government revenue. Roosevelt insisted on this design to separate Social Security from the stigma of welfare; “No dole,” he said repeatedly.

cards.a: The attack on Pearl Harbor turned two regional wars into a true world war and committed the United States to global leadership.

cards.q: What led to Attack on Pearl Harbor?
cards.a: Facing severe shortages, unwilling to leave China, and convinced that American officials opposed further talks, Japan’s leaders decided to strike first. Their planners hoped to destroy enough battleships and aircraft carriers to cripple American naval power while Japan seized resource-rich territories in Southeast Asia.
Japanese aircraft struck the fleet at anchor. The battleship USS Arizona was sunk with the loss of 1,177 crew members; more than 900 of them remain entombed in the ship.

cards.q: Why does World War II matter?
cards.a: World War II was the most destructive conflict in history. It defeated fascism and Nazism through the combined efforts of the Allies; the Soviet Union, at a cost of some 24 to 25 million lives, broke the German army, while Britain and the United States fought in the west and the Pacific.

After Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor, fear of espionage and sabotage swept the West Coast, intensified by long-standing anti-Asian racism and economic rivalry. Political pressure grew to remove Japanese Americans, both immigrants and citizens.

The order justified itself by “the successful prosecution of the war,” which it said “requires every possible protection against espionage and against sabotage.” It delegated broad power to the military to decide who could live where, without hearings or charges.

cards.a: Hiroshima and Nagasaki ended the deadliest war in history and made the prospect of nuclear annihilation a permanent feature of world politics.

cards.q: What led to Atomic Bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki?
cards.a: After the bloody battles of Iwo Jima and Okinawa, U.S. officials expected Japanese forces to fight fiercely for their home islands; some estimated that an invasion could cost half a million American casualties and perhaps millions of Japanese civilians. These estimates were later cited to justify the bombings.

Hiroshima. Hiroshima, a city of almost 300,000 civilians and an important military center, was the primary target. At about 8:15 a.m. on August 6, the B-29 Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets, released “Little Boy,” which exploded 1,900 feet above the city.

cards.q: What can it do, and what limits it?
cards.a: The Charter created a General Assembly of all member states; a Security Council with five permanent members, each holding a veto, and elected non-permanent members; an Economic and Social Council; an International Court of Justice; a Trusteeship Council to oversee certain colonial territories; and a Secretariat headed by a Secretary-General.

cards.q: Why does the Cold War matter?
cards.a: For more than four decades the Cold War defined world politics. It divided Europe, spread conflict and competition to every continent, and produced the nuclear arms race and the space race.
The Soviet Union and the United States had been allies against Germany, but the alliance rested on necessity.

The Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan (1947–1948): committed the United States to containing Soviet influence in Europe. 1949: the end of the Berlin blockade, the founding of NATO, the first Soviet atomic bomb, and the communist victory in China. The Korean War (1950–1953): turned containment into a global military commitment. Sputnik (1957): opened the space race and shocked Americans into investing in science and rockets. The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962): the moment the superpowers came closest to nuclear war, followed by the first arms control agreements. The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the end of the Soviet Union (1991).

cards.q: Why does the Marshall Plan matter?
cards.a: The Marshall Plan was one of the most ambitious and successful foreign policy initiatives in American history, binding Western Europe to the United States at the start of the Cold War.

cards.q: What led to the Marshall Plan?
cards.a: Coming just months after the Truman Doctrine, Marshall’s proposal argued that the United States should help restore “normal economic health to the world, without which there can be no political stability and no assured peace.”

American aid poured into Western Europe for reconstruction while trade barriers were loosened. Participation by the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe was initially possible, but Stalin, suspicious of American economic domination and unwilling to open Soviet society to Westerners, refused.

Korea was the first “hot” war of the Cold War — a limited war fought to contain communism without triggering a wider conflict with the Soviet Union or China.

At the end of World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union divided Korea at the 38th parallel to accept the surrender of Japanese forces. The Soviets backed a communist government in the North; the United States backed Rhee in the South.

The Inchon landing (September 1950): reversed the North Korean invasion. Chinese entry (late 1950): turned a near-victory into a long, bloody stalemate. MacArthur’s dismissal (April 1951): affirmed civilian control of the military and the decision to keep the war limited.

cards.a: McCarthyism showed how fear of an external enemy could be turned against Americans’ own civil liberties.

cards.q: What led to McCarthyism and the Second Red Scare?

On February 9, 1950, in Wheeling, West Virginia, McCarthy declared he had a list of 205 State Department employees who were members of the Communist Party. He had no such list; the number changed to 57, then 81.

cards.a: Brown ended the constitutional legitimacy of legal segregation and gave the civil rights movement its foundation in law, even though its promise took decades to fulfill.

cards.q: Why does the Civil Rights Movement matter?
cards.a: The civil rights movement ended legal segregation in the United States, brought about the greatest change in federal protection of voting since Reconstruction, and showed how ordinary people using nonviolent mass action could change the law of a nation.

The movement set out to destroy Jim Crow, the system of laws and customs that segregated Black Southerners in schools, buses, restaurants, parks, and jobs and kept most of them from voting. After World War II, the “Double V” campaign for victory over fascism abroad and racism at home, and the postwar boom, raised expectations that persistent segregation then disappointed. The demands of the 1963 March on Washington summed up the movement’s program: a comprehensive civil rights bill ending segregated public accommodations, “protection of the right to vote,” “desegregation of all public schools,” a federal jobs program, and a law “barring discrimination in all employment.” King described the ultimate end as “the creation of the beloved community,” “a society at peace with itself, a society that can live with its conscience”; by the end of his life he argued that full citizenship also required economic security.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: In the courts. Beginning in the early 1930s, NAACP lawyers including Charles Hamilton Houston and Thurgood Marshall chose cases on education, voting, and juries to wear away the legal foundations of segregation, first arguing that Southern states failed to provide even “equal” facilities and then, by the late 1940s, that separation itself was unconstitutional. Brown v. Board of Education combined five cases from South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware, Washington, D.C., and Kansas.

cards.q: Why does Montgomery Bus Boycott matter?
cards.a: Montgomery proved that ordinary people acting together could defeat Jim Crow, and it introduced Martin Luther King Jr. to the nation.

cards.q: What led to Montgomery Bus Boycott?
cards.a: On the evening of December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, a forty-two-year-old seamstress at the Montgomery Fair department store who was active in the local NAACP, was sitting in the first row behind the white section. When the bus filled, driver James Blake ordered her row to stand.

On December 5 about 90 percent of Montgomery’s Black citizens stayed off the buses. That afternoon, at Mt. Zion AME Church, leaders formed the Montgomery Improvement Association to continue the protest and elected King, new to the city, as president.

cards.q: Why does the Space Race matter?
cards.a: The space race turned science and engineering into instruments of Cold War competition, created NASA, and poured billions of dollars into research. Its triumph, the moon landing, restored American confidence after years of Soviet firsts.

cards.q: What led to the Space Race?
cards.a: The contest grew out of the Cold War rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their competing ideologies. Each side wanted to prove its technological and military strength to the world — and the Soviet Union, with powerful rockets developed under the engineer Sergei Korolev, struck first.
Sputnik caught the American public off guard. A month later Sputnik 2 carried a dog, Laika, into orbit; she died soon after launch.

cards.a: Red Power made Native Americans’ demands for sovereignty visible to the nation and reshaped federal Indian policy.
Activists demanded respect for treaty rights, tribal sovereignty and self-determination, return of land, and an end to discrimination and to federal efforts to dissolve tribes.

cards.a: In 1961 Native university students founded the National Indian Youth Council, whose militant rhetoric and direct action began the Red Power movement. In 1964 it held “fish-ins” in the Pacific Northwest, casting nets in defiance of state laws to defend tribal fishing rights.

Second-wave feminism transformed women’s legal status and opportunities and changed American expectations about work, family, and equality.

Feminists sought equal treatment in employment and pay, an end to sex discrimination in law, access to contraception and abortion, child care, equality in marriage, and the Equal Rights Amendment, which declared that “equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged … on account of sex.”

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: Some women worked through institutions: President Kennedy’s Commission on the Status of Women, chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, documented discrimination in a 1963 report. Friedan’s best-selling The Feminine Mystique named “the problem that has no name” — the dissatisfaction of many middle-class housewives.

cards.q: Why does the Cuban Missile Crisis matter?
cards.a: The crisis brought the world to the edge of nuclear war and then pushed both superpowers to step back: they set up a direct line of communication and took the first steps toward controlling the nuclear arms race.

cards.q: What led to the Cuban Missile Crisis?
cards.a: The crisis grew out of the arms race and the Cold War rivalry over Cuba. The Soviets wanted to protect Castro’s government, to compete with China for the loyalty of revolutionaries worldwide, and to neutralize the large American advantage in nuclear weapons.

On October 14 a U-2 took pictures clearly showing sites for medium- and intermediate-range nuclear missiles; the next day the photographs reached the White House. Kennedy gathered his closest advisers in secret meetings.

cards.q: Why does the Environmental Movement matter?
cards.a: The environmental movement made protecting nature and public health a permanent responsibility of the federal government.

Environmentalists sought clean air and water, controls on pesticides and toxic chemicals, protection of wilderness and wildlife, and government accountability for the environmental effects of its projects.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: The movement grew from Americans’ postwar enjoyment of the outdoors and from science-based warnings like Carson’s. Dramatic events — such as the Cuyahoga River near Cleveland bursting into flames — drew attention.

cards.q: Why does the Farm Workers Movement matter?
cards.a: The farm workers’ struggle joined labor organizing to the civil rights movement and made Chicano and Filipino workers visible in national politics.

Farm workers sought union recognition, higher wages (grape pickers averaged about 90 cents an hour in 1965), an end to child labor and dangerous conditions, protection from pesticides, and fair treatment. Chavez envisioned the union as both a labor organization and a civil rights movement for Chicano and Filipino workers.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: On September 8, 1965, Filipino workers of the AWOC, organized by Larry Itliong, struck nine farms near Delano. The NFWA voted to join on September 16.

cards.a: The March on Washington joined the moral appeal of the civil rights movement to its economic demands. It showed the nation the movement’s size, discipline, and breadth, and it gave King’s dream of racial equality its most lasting expression.

cards.q: What led to March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom?
cards.a: The march’s official goals, as listed by the King Institute and the American Yawp, were a comprehensive civil rights bill ending segregation in public accommodations, protection of the right to vote, desegregation of all public schools in 1963, a federal works program to train and place unemployed workers, a federal fair employment law, and a higher minimum wage. Its full name, the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, reflected the economic demands at its heart, which came from Randolph’s labor background.

cards.a: The Civil Rights Act ended legal segregation in public life across the South and gave the federal government new power to fight discrimination in schools and workplaces. Politically, the Yawp notes, it and the Voting Rights Act helped drive the rise of Republicans in the South and West.

cards.a: The Great Society expanded the federal government’s responsibility for health, education, and poverty more than any reform program since the New Deal.

cards.a: Johnson, shaped by the New Deal and by his own family’s poverty in the Texas Hill Country, believed government could abolish poverty and racial injustice in an age of affluence.

cards.q: Why does the Vietnam War matter?
cards.a: The Vietnam War was a defeat for American Cold War policy and a turning point in American history. It divided a generation, undermined faith in government, and made Americans wary of foreign wars for decades.

Vietnam had been ruled by France since the nineteenth century and was occupied by Japan during World War II. In 1945 the nationalist leader Ho Chi Minh declared Vietnam’s independence, quoting the American Declaration of Independence.

Dien Bien Phu (1954): the French defeat led to the partition of Vietnam and deepening American involvement. The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964): gave Johnson a free hand to escalate the war. The Tet Offensive (1968): a military setback for the communists but a political turning point that turned many Americans against the war. Johnson’s withdrawal from the 1968 race: marked the end of escalation. The Paris Peace Accords (1973): ended direct American participation.

cards.a: Selma turned the right to vote into a national cause and produced one of the most consequential laws in American history.

cards.a: On February 18, during a night march in nearby Marion, a state trooper shot Jimmie Lee Jackson, a 26-year-old church deacon, as he tried to protect his mother; he died eight days later. Activists resolved to march from Selma to the state capitol in Montgomery.

On Sunday, March 7, marchers crossed the Edmund Pettus Bridge and met a wall of state troopers and lawmen, who ordered them to disperse and then attacked, cheered on by white onlookers. John Lewis was severely beaten.

cards.q: Why does Voting Rights Act of 1965 matter?
cards.a: The Voting Rights Act finally enforced the Fifteenth Amendment and transformed Southern politics. The American Yawp writes that together with the Civil Rights Act of 1964 it “effectively ended Jim Crow.” Johnson called the vote “the most powerful instrument ever devised by man for breaking down injustice.”

The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) forbade denying the vote on account of race, but from the 1890s Southern states had used literacy tests, poll taxes, and other devices to keep Black citizens from voting. Those who tried to register risked harassment, economic reprisals, and violence, and Black registration and political power stayed low. In the summer of 1964 three voting rights workers were murdered in Mississippi during Freedom Summer.
Section 2 applied nationwide. Closely following the Fifteenth Amendment, it forbade denying or abridging the right to vote on account of race or color.

cards.q: Why does Miranda v. Arizona matter?
cards.a: Miranda turned a constitutional principle into a concrete practice that protects people at the moment they are most vulnerable to the power of the state.

Chief Justice Earl Warren
One year in jail, suspended if the Lovings left Virginia for 25 years
Fourteenth Amendment: Equal Protection and Due Process

cards.q: Why does Loving v. Virginia matter?
cards.a: Loving struck down a major legal pillar of racial segregation and affirmed marriage as a basic civil right.

cards.q: What question did the Court have to answer?
cards.a: Did Virginia’s law banning interracial marriage violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment?
Yes. The Court unanimously struck down the law under both the Equal Protection Clause and the Due Process Clause.

cards.a: The first human landing on the Moon, July 1969

cards.a: Apollo 11
July 16, 1969, Cape Kennedy
Neil Armstrong (commander), Michael Collins (command module pilot), Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin (lunar module pilot)
July 20, 1969, Sea of Tranquility
An estimated 650 million people
July 24, 1969, Pacific Ocean, 13 miles from USS Hornet
Apollo 11 fulfilled a national goal, gave the United States a decisive symbolic victory in the Cold War space race, and gave the world a shared moment of wonder.
The space race was a Cold War contest for prestige and technological leadership.
Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969. On July 20, Eagle separated from Columbia and, partly piloted by hand by Armstrong, landed in the Sea of Tranquility.

entries.title: Woodstock
entries.subtitle: “3 Days of Peace and Music” that came to define a generation

cards.a: “3 Days of Peace and Music” that came to define a generation
August 1969 · Bethel, New York

cards.q: Name it: “3 Days of Peace and Music” that came to define a generation
cards.a: Woodstock
Three days in August 1969
Yasgur’s farm, Bethel, New York
Nearly half a million people
“An Aquarian Exposition: 3 Days of Peace and Music”
Woodstock is remembered as the high point of the 1960s counterculture — a symbol of a generation that challenged the values of its parents.

The festival took place weeks after Americans first walked on the Moon, against the backdrop of a nation divided over the Vietnam War, civil rights, and sexual politics. PBS describes a sense of an America in transition — a handoff between generations with very different values and ideals.

Over three days, a crowd of nearly half a million — rain-soaked, often hungry, many of them on drugs — turned a few acres of farmland into a swarming, impromptu city. PBS’s American Experience calls what happened “nothing less than a miracle of teamwork,” a demonstration of the “peace and love” the festival had promised.

cards.a: The Watergate Scandal

Hush money; the CIA asked to halt the FBI investigation

cards.q: Why does the Watergate Scandal matter?
cards.a: Watergate showed both how a president could abuse power and how the press, Congress, and the courts could hold him to account.

cards.q: What led to the Watergate Scandal?
cards.a: Five men, one a former CIA employee working as a security aide for the Committee to Re-elect the President, were caught installing bugging equipment at the Democratic headquarters.

Officials paid hush money to the burglars and White House aides, and Nixon won a landslide reelection in November 1972. Reporting by Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein of the Washington Post kept linking the burglary to the White House.

entries.subtitle: The 1973 decision recognizing a constitutional right to abortion, overruled in 2022

cards.a: The 1973 decision recognizing a constitutional right to abortion, overruled in 2022

cards.a: Roe v. Wade

Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, June 24, 2022

cards.q: Why does Roe v. Wade matter?
cards.a: Roe and its reversal in Dobbs framed half a century of debate over privacy, women’s equality, and the role of the courts.

cards.q: What question did the Court have to answer?
cards.a: Does the Constitution recognize a woman’s right to terminate her pregnancy by abortion?
Yes. The Due Process Clause protects a right to privacy that includes the abortion decision.

cards.a: The Supreme Court orders the president to release the Watergate tapes

cards.a: United States v. Nixon
8–0 (Justice William Rehnquist did not participate)
Chief Justice Warren Burger
Executive privilege vs. a criminal trial subpoena
Nixon released the tapes and resigned August 9, 1974

cards.q: Why does United States v. Nixon matter?
cards.a: United States v. Nixon affirmed that no one, including the president, is beyond the reach of the courts.

cards.q: What question did the Court have to answer?
cards.a: Is the president’s executive privilege entirely immune from judicial review?

No. The Court held that neither the separation of powers nor the general need for confidentiality could sustain an absolute, unqualified presidential privilege in the face of a criminal subpoena. Nixon had to produce the tapes.

entries.title: The End of the Cold War
entries.subtitle: The fall of communism in Eastern Europe and the collapse of the Soviet Union, 1989–1991

cards.q: What was the End of the Cold War?
cards.a: The fall of communism in Eastern Europe and the collapse of the Soviet Union, 1989–1991
1989 – December 25, 1991 · Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union

cards.q: Name it: The fall of communism in Eastern Europe and the collapse of the Soviet Union, 1989–1991
cards.a: The End of the Cold War
1987: Reagan and Gorbachev agree to reduce nuclear arsenals
Solidarity wins elections, June 4, 1989
Opened November 9, 1989
August 1991, against Gorbachev

cards.q: Why does the End of the Cold War matter?
cards.a: The peaceful end of the Cold War closed a four-decade conflict that had shaped American life and lifted the threat of superpower nuclear war.

cards.q: What led to the End of the Cold War?
cards.a: Gorbachev, who came to power in 1985, believed the Soviet system needed reform and sought to end the ruinous arms race. He met Reagan at Geneva in 1985 and Reykjavik in 1986, and the two signed the Intermediate Nuclear Forces Treaty in 1987.

In Poland, round-table talks with the banned union Solidarity led to elections on June 4, 1989, which Solidarity won overwhelmingly; by August the country had Eastern Europe’s first non-communist prime minister. Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Romania, Bulgaria, and East Germany followed.

entries.title: Persian Gulf War
entries.subtitle: The U.S.-led coalition that expelled Iraq from Kuwait, 1990–1991

cards.a: The U.S.-led coalition that expelled Iraq from Kuwait, 1990–1991
August 2, 1990 – February 28, 1991 · Kuwait, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia

cards.a: Persian Gulf War
August 2, 1990: some 100,000 Iraqi troops overran Kuwait
Resolution 678 authorized force if Iraq did not withdraw
Began January 1991
February 24–28, 1991
Kuwait liberated; Saddam Hussein remained in power

cards.q: Why does Persian Gulf War matter?
cards.a: The Gulf War demonstrated American military dominance after the Cold War and began a long U.S. military involvement in the Persian Gulf.

Iraq emerged from its 1980–1988 war with Iran deeply in debt, owing some $37 billion to Gulf creditors. Saddam Hussein demanded that Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates forgive Iraq’s loans, accused Kuwait of overproducing oil and stealing from a shared oil field, and revived old territorial claims.
UN Resolution 678: gave the coalition international legal authority. Air supremacy in the first days of Desert Storm: crippled Iraq’s ability to fight.

entries.title: September 11 Attacks
entries.subtitle: The al-Qaeda terrorist attacks of 2001

cards.a: The al-Qaeda terrorist attacks of 2001
September 11, 2001 · New York City; Arlington, Virginia; near Shanksville, Pennsylvania
Nineteen al-Qaeda operatives
North Tower hit 8:46 a.m.; South Tower 9:03 a.m.; both collapsed
Struck at 9:37 a.m.
Crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at 10:03 a.m. after passengers revolted
More than 2,600 at the WTC, 125 at the Pentagon, 256 on the planes
September 11 was the defining event of the early twenty-first century for the United States, transforming its foreign policy and sense of security.

Bin Laden’s radical Islamist ideology cast the United States as the enemy of Muslims. The 9/11 Commission later concluded that the attacks were “a shock, but they should not have come as a surprise,” citing failures of imagination, policy, capabilities, and management across the government.
American Airlines Flight 11 crashed into the North Tower of the World Trade Center at 8:46 a.m., and United Flight 175 into the South Tower at 9:03. American Flight 77 struck the Pentagon at 9:37.

entries.title: War in Afghanistan
entries.subtitle: America’s longest war, 2001–2021

cards.a: America’s longest war, 2001–2021
October 7, 2001 – August 2021 · Afghanistan and the Pakistan border region
War in Afghanistan
October 7, 2001 (Operation Enduring Freedom)
November 13, 2001
2009: 17,000 additional U.S. troops
May 2011, in a raid in Pakistan
August 2021; the Taliban returned to power

cards.q: Why does War in Afghanistan matter?
cards.a: Afghanistan, America’s longest war, showed both the reach of U.S. military power and its limits in remaking another society.

During the 1980s the United States armed the Mujahideen resisting the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan; Osama bin Laden also fought with them. After the Soviets withdrew in 1989, civil war followed, and the Taliban took power in 1996 and sheltered al-Qaeda.

The fall of Kabul (November 2001): toppled the Taliban but let al-Qaeda’s leaders escape. The shift to Iraq (2003): drew U.S. resources away as the Taliban regrouped. Bin Laden’s death (2011): fulfilled a central goal and opened the way to drawdown.

entries.title: Iraq War
entries.subtitle: The U.S. invasion and occupation of Iraq, 2003–2011

cards.a: The U.S. invasion and occupation of Iraq, 2003–2011
March 20, 2003 – December 18, 2011 · Iraq
October 2002
Bombing of Baghdad began March 20, 2003; Baghdad fell April 9
None were found
Captured December 13, 2003; executed December 30, 2006
Last combat forces left December 18, 2011
The Iraq War became a cautionary tale about preventive war, faulty intelligence, and the difficulty of occupation.
After the 1991 Gulf War, the United States maintained sanctions, weapons inspections, and no-fly zones over Iraq. In 1998 President Clinton ordered strikes on suspected weapons sites.

The fall of Baghdad (April 2003): a quick conventional victory that gave way to occupation. The failure to find WMD: undermined the war’s justification. The surge (2007): reduced violence and enabled withdrawal.

entries.title: The Great Recession
entries.subtitle: The financial crisis and deep recession of 2007–2009

cards.a: The financial crisis and deep recession of 2007–2009
December 2007 – June 2009 · Nationwide and worldwide
Real GDP fell 4.3 percent, the largest postwar decline
From 5 percent (December 2007) to a peak of 10 percent (October 2009)
Home prices fell about 30 percent from mid-2006 to mid-2009
S&P 500 fell 57 percent from October 2007 to March 2009

cards.q: Why does the Great Recession matter?
cards.a: The Great Recession was the longest recession since World War II, with the largest drop in output of the postwar era, and a defining event for a generation of Americans.

cards.q: What led to the Great Recession?
cards.a: The housing boom peaked in 2006. As prices fell and homeowners defaulted, losses spread through the heavily leveraged financial system, because mortgages had been bundled and resold so often that it was hard to tell who owned what.

Major firms such as Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers disappeared almost overnight. President George W. Bush signed the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act, and the government poured billions into propping up banks.

entries.title: COVID-19 Pandemic
entries.subtitle: The coronavirus pandemic in the United States, 2020–2023

cards.a: The coronavirus pandemic in the United States, 2020–2023
January 20, 2020 · Nationwide and worldwide

By the World Health Organization, March 11, 2020
Declared March 13, 2020; CARES Act signed March 27, 2020
December 11, 2020 (Pfizer-BioNTech)
More than one million by May 2022
With more than a million American deaths, COVID-19 was a defining experience of the early twenty-first century.
Despite a lockdown in Wuhan on January 23, 2020, the virus spread worldwide through travel.
The CDC confirmed the first U.S. case on January 20, 2020. On March 11 the WHO declared a pandemic, and on March 13 the Trump administration declared a national emergency.

entries.title: Abigail Adams
entries.subtitle: Political partner, letter writer, and early voice for women’s rights

cards.a: Political partner, letter writer, and early voice for women’s rights. Correspondent and political adviser to John Adams; Manager of the Adams farm and finances; First Lady (1797–1801); Mother of President John Quincy Adams
Born November 22, 1744, Weymouth, Massachusetts; died October 28, 1818, Quincy, Massachusetts

cards.q: Who is this? Political partner, letter writer, and early voice for women’s rights
cards.a: Abigail Adams
John Adams, in 1764
Including John Quincy Adams, the sixth president
March 31, 1776, to John Adams at the Continental Congress
By her grandson Charles Francis Adams in 1848

Through her letters, Abigail Adams gives us one of the clearest views of the Revolution from inside a household, and her call to “Remember the Ladies” is an early marker in the long history of American women’s rights.

cards.q: What shaped Abigail Adams early in life?
cards.a: Abigail Smith was born on November 22, 1744, in Weymouth, Massachusetts, the daughter of the Reverend William Smith, a Congregational minister.

cards.q: What were Abigail Adams’s major achievements?
cards.a: When John went to the Continental Congress in 1774, and then to Europe as a diplomat from 1778, Abigail stayed in Braintree and served as what the National Women’s History Museum calls a “deputy husband.”

entries.title: Abraham Lincoln
entries.subtitle: Sixteenth president, who preserved the Union and ended slavery

cards.a: Sixteenth president, who preserved the Union and ended slavery. Illinois lawyer and legislator; U.S. representative (1847–1849); Sixteenth president (1861–1865); First Republican president
Born February 12, 1809, Hardin County, Kentucky; died April 15, 1865, Washington, D.C.

cards.q: Who is this? Sixteenth president, who preserved the Union and ended slavery
cards.a: Abraham Lincoln
February 12, 1809, in a one-room log cabin in Hardin County, Kentucky
Whig, then Republican from 1856; the first Republican president
Seven debates in the 1858 Illinois Senate race, which he lost but which made him a national figure
1860 (180 electoral votes of 303) and 1864 (55 percent of the popular vote)
House Divided (1858), Gettysburg Address (1863), Second Inaugural (1865)
Shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford’s Theatre on April 14, 1865; died the next morning

Lincoln saved the Union and destroyed slavery, and he did both by appealing to the nation’s founding ideals, above all the Declaration’s promise that all men are created equal. His wartime presidency also transformed the office, setting precedents for presidential power in a national emergency that historians still debate.

cards.q: What shaped Abraham Lincoln early in life?
cards.a: Abraham Lincoln was born on February 12, 1809, in a one-room log cabin with a dirt floor in Hardin County, Kentucky. His father, Thomas, a farmer and carpenter who could barely sign his name, moved the family to the Indiana frontier when Abraham was seven.

cards.q: What were Abraham Lincoln’s major achievements?
cards.a: As a young legislator Lincoln was one of only six members, out of eighty-three, who voted against a 1837 resolution condemning abolitionists. Elected to Congress in 1846, he challenged President James Polk’s claim that Mexico had started the Mexican-American War on American soil, an unpopular stand at home, and served only a single term. After several years practicing law, he returned to politics in 1854, and in 1856 he joined the new Republican Party, which was dedicated to repealing the Kansas-Nebraska Act and stopping the spread of slavery into the West.

entries.title: Alcatraz Island
entries.subtitle: San Francisco Bay island: a prison, then the site of the 1969–1971 Indian occupation

cards.a: San Francisco Bay island: a prison, then the site of the 1969–1971 Indian occupation
San Francisco Bay, California (Golden Gate National Recreation Area) · West
March 9, 1964: five Sicangu Lakota landed for four hours, citing the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty
November 20, 1969 – June 11, 1971
Indians of All Tribes; about 100 at first, including 80 UCLA students
Richard Oakes (Akwesasne Mohawk)
Golden Gate National Recreation Area, National Park Service

Though the occupiers did not win the island, the Park Service concludes that the occupation helped end the federal termination policy and gave birth to a lasting political movement for Indian self-determination.
Alcatraz is a rocky island in San Francisco Bay. It served for many years as a prison holding both military prisoners and civilians.

Before the prison. Ohlone people lived around San Francisco Bay for thousands of years; oral history suggests Alcatraz was used to isolate tribal members who had broken laws, to gather bird eggs and sea life, and as a hiding place for Indians escaping the Spanish missions.

entries.title: Alexander Hamilton
entries.subtitle: First secretary of the Treasury and architect of the federal financial system

cards.a: First secretary of the Treasury and architect of the federal financial system. Aide-de-camp to George Washington (1777–1781); Member of the Continental Congress; Delegate to the Constitutional Convention (1787); Principal author of the Federalist Papers; First secretary of the Treasury (1789–1795); Lawyer in New York City
Born January 11, 1757 (disputed), Charlestown, Nevis, British West Indies; died July 12, 1804, New York City

cards.q: Who is this? First secretary of the Treasury and architect of the federal financial system
cards.a: Alexander Hamilton
January 11, 1757 (or perhaps 1755), Charlestown, Nevis, British West Indies
Artillery captain in 1776; aide-de-camp to Washington, March 1777 to February 1781
Helped call the Constitutional Convention; wrote most of the 85 Federalist essays
First secretary of the Treasury, 1789–1795: debt funding, assumption of state debts, the Bank, excise taxes
Married Elizabeth Schuyler during the Revolution; built The Grange in upper Manhattan, completed in 1802
Mortally wounded by Aaron Burr in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey, July 11, 1804; died July 12
Hamilton designed the financial foundations of the federal government.

cards.q: What shaped Alexander Hamilton early in life?
cards.a: Alexander Hamilton was born in Charlestown on the Caribbean island of Nevis, in the British West Indies.

cards.q: What were Alexander Hamilton’s major achievements?
cards.a: Making the Constitution. Hamilton believed the Articles of Confederation left the nation dangerously weak.

entries.title: Amelia Earhart
entries.subtitle: The first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, who vanished over the Pacific in 1937

cards.a: The first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, who vanished over the Pacific in 1937. Aviator; Author and lecturer; Career adviser at Purdue University (1935–1937)
Born 1897, Atchison, Kansas; died July 2, 1937, Disappeared near Howland Island, Pacific Ocean

cards.q: Who is this? The first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, who vanished over the Pacific in 1937
cards.a: Amelia Earhart
June 1928: the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air
May 20–21, 1932, Newfoundland to Ireland — the first woman, and the second person after Lindbergh
The Distinguished Flying Cross, the first awarded to a woman
January 11, 1935: first person to fly solo from Honolulu to Oakland
July 2, 1937, with navigator Fred Noonan, on the flight from Lae, New Guinea, to Howland Island

Earhart turned aviation into a cause for women’s equality, proving in the most public way possible that women could match men in skill and daring. Her unexplained disappearance made her a lasting American legend.

cards.q: What shaped Amelia Earhart early in life?
cards.a: Amelia Mary Earhart was born in Atchison, Kansas, in 1897. As a girl she climbed trees, “belly slammed” her sled downhill, and hunted rats with a .22 rifle, and she kept a scrapbook about women succeeding in fields dominated by men.

cards.q: What were Amelia Earhart’s major achievements?
cards.a: In April 1928 the publisher George P. Putnam’s team asked her, “How would you like to be the first woman to fly the Atlantic?”

entries.title: Andrew Carnegie
entries.subtitle: Steel magnate and philanthropist of the Gilded Age

cards.a: Steel magnate and philanthropist of the Gilded Age. Telegrapher and railroad manager; Founder of Carnegie Steel; Philanthropist; author of “The Gospel of Wealth”
Born 1835, Dunfermline, Scotland; died 1919

cards.q: Who is this? Steel magnate and philanthropist of the Gilded Age
cards.a: Andrew Carnegie
1848, at age 13, from Dunfermline, Scotland, to Allegheny, Pennsylvania
Bobbin boy in a cotton mill, $1.20 a week
1901, to J. P. Morgan, forming U.S. Steel
About half of America’s public libraries had been built with his money by his death in 1919

Carnegie’s rise from immigrant mill boy to steel king made him the era’s emblem of the self-made man, while Homestead and his philanthropy raised enduring questions about wealth, power, and responsibility.

cards.q: What shaped Andrew Carnegie early in life?
cards.a: Carnegie was born in 1835 in a one-room house in Dunfermline, Scotland, the son of a handloom weaver. When machines took over weaving in the 1840s the family was impoverished, and in 1848 his strong-willed mother led them to Allegheny, Pennsylvania.

cards.q: What were Andrew Carnegie’s major achievements?
cards.a: Mentored by Scott, who helped him invest — often in insider deals — Carnegie was rich by the end of the Civil War. He bet on steel.

entries.title: Andrew Jackson
entries.subtitle: Seventh president, champion of the “common man,” and architect of Indian removal

cards.a: Seventh president, champion of the “common man,” and architect of Indian removal. Tennessee congressman, senator, and judge; Major general in the War of 1812; Territorial governor of Florida (1821); Seventh president (1829–1837); Founder of the Democratic Party; Tennessee planter and enslaver
Born March 15, 1767, Waxhaw settlement, on the North Carolina–South Carolina border; died June 8, 1845, The Hermitage, near Nashville, Tennessee

cards.q: Who is this? Seventh president, champion of the “common man,” and architect of Indian removal
cards.a: Andrew Jackson
March 15, 1767, Waxhaw settlement on the Carolina border (the exact birthplace is disputed)
Defeated the Red Stick Creeks at Horseshoe Bend (March 1814) and the British at New Orleans (January 8, 1815)
Lost in the House in 1824 despite leading the vote; won 1828 (178 electoral votes to 83) and 1832 (219 to 49)
Signed the Indian Removal Act, May 28, 1830
Vetoed recharter of the Second Bank, July 10, 1832; removed federal deposits, 1833
Twelve, more than his six predecessors combined
Jackson turned the presidency into a direct link between the president and the voters and built the first modern mass party, while his opponents organized as the Whigs.

cards.q: What shaped Andrew Jackson early in life?
cards.a: Andrew Jackson was born on March 15, 1767, in the Waxhaw settlement, a community of Scotch-Irish immigrants on the border between North and South Carolina. His exact birthplace is disputed, but he considered himself a South Carolinian. His father died before he was born. The Revolution wiped out the rest of his family.

cards.q: What were Andrew Jackson’s major achievements?
cards.a: The road to the White House. In 1824 Jackson led a four-man field with 43 percent of the popular vote and 99 electoral votes, short of a majority.

entries.title: Babe Ruth
entries.subtitle: The slugger who transformed baseball and became the most celebrated athlete of the 1920s

cards.a: The slugger who transformed baseball and became the most celebrated athlete of the 1920s. Pitcher, Boston Red Sox (1914–1919); Outfielder, New York Yankees (1920–1934); Boston Braves (1935); One of the first five members of the Baseball Hall of Fame (1936)
Born February 6, 1895, Baltimore, Maryland; died August 16, 1948, New York City

cards.q: Who is this? The slugger who transformed baseball and became the most celebrated athlete of the 1920s
cards.a: Babe Ruth
714 home runs, a .342 batting average, and 2,214 runs batted in over 22 seasons
89 wins in six seasons with the Red Sox; a record 29⅔ straight scoreless World Series innings
Sold by the Red Sox to the Yankees for $100,000 after the 1919 season
His single-season home run record stood for 34 years
Seven: three with Boston, four with New York
One of the first five players elected, in 1936

Ruth changed how baseball was played — from a game of singles and stolen bases to one built on power — and, with the help of a ravenous press, made sports stardom a national obsession. He remains the standard against which American athletic greatness is measured.

cards.q: What shaped Babe Ruth early in life?
cards.a: George Herman Ruth was born on February 6, 1895, in Baltimore. His father ran a saloon and his mother was often ill, and by the age of six “Little George” was roaming the waterfront unsupervised, stealing, vandalizing, and drinking the dregs from beer glasses in his father’s bar.

cards.q: What were Babe Ruth’s major achievements?
cards.a: Ruth was first a superb left-handed pitcher. He won 23 games in 1916 with a league-leading 1.75 earned run average, pitched all fourteen innings of a World Series victory, and helped Boston win three championships.

entries.title: Barack Obama
entries.subtitle: Forty-fourth president and the first African American president

cards.a: Forty-fourth president and the first African American president. Community organizer, Chicago; President of the Harvard Law Review; Illinois state senator (1997–2004); U.S. Senator from Illinois (2005–2008); Forty-fourth president (2009–2017)
Born August 4, 1961, Hawaii

cards.q: Who is this? Forty-fourth president and the first African American president
cards.a: Barack Obama
Occidental College; Columbia University (1983); Harvard Law School, magna cum laude
Community organizer; civil rights lawyer; Illinois state senator; U.S. senator (2005–2008)
2008: defeated John McCain, 365 electoral votes to 173; 2012: defeated Mitt Romney, 332 to 206
American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (2009); Affordable Care Act (March 23, 2010); Dodd-Frank (2010)
Withdrawal from Iraq; killing of Osama bin Laden (May 2, 2011); Iran nuclear agreement (2015); Paris climate agreement (2015)

Obama’s election was a landmark in the long history of race in American politics. His presidency also pulled the economy back from the edge of a second depression and changed the American health-care system.

cards.q: What shaped Barack Obama early in life?
cards.a: Barack Hussein Obama II was born in Hawaii on August 4, 1961. His parents, who had met as students at the University of Hawaii, were Ann Dunham, a white American from Kansas, and Barack Obama Sr., a Black Kenyan studying in the United States. His father left the family when Obama was two and later returned to Kenya.

cards.q: What were Barack Obama’s major achievements?
cards.a: The 2008 election. Obama announced his candidacy in February 2007.

entries.title: Benjamin Franklin
entries.subtitle: Printer, scientist, diplomat, and the Revolution’s elder statesman

cards.a: Printer, scientist, diplomat, and the Revolution’s elder statesman. Printer and publisher; Scientist and inventor; Deputy postmaster general for the colonies; Colonial agent in London (1757–1775); Diplomat and minister to France; Signer of the Declaration, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution; President of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society
Born January 17, 1706, Boston, Massachusetts; died April 17, 1790, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

cards.q: Who is this? Printer, scientist, diplomat, and the Revolution’s elder statesman
cards.a: Benjamin Franklin
Published the Pennsylvania Gazette and Poor Richard’s Almanack (1732–1757)
Showed that lightning is electrical; invented the lightning rod, the Franklin stove, bifocals, and the glass armonica
Colonial agent, 1757–1775; helped win repeal of the Stamp Act (1766)
Commissioner from 1776; first American minister received by a foreign government (1779)
Declaration of Independence (1776), Treaty of Paris (1783), Constitution (1787)

Franklin signed the three documents that established the nation, the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution, and the State Department’s historians call him the most distinguished scientific and literary American of the colonial era. His life became a model of the self-made American, and his civic projects, scientific work, and diplomacy helped shape both colonial society and the new nation.

cards.q: What shaped Benjamin Franklin early in life?
cards.a: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston on January 17, 1706, to Josiah Franklin, a maker of candles and soap, and Abiah Folger. Lehigh University’s exhibit calls him the tenth child, and the Library of Congress the tenth son. He had only about two years of schooling.

cards.q: What were Benjamin Franklin’s major achievements?
cards.a: Scientist and inventor. Franklin’s electrical experiments, published as Experiments and Observations on Electricity, set out a theory of positive and negative charge, argued that lightning was electrical, and proposed a tall, grounded rod to protect buildings.

entries.title: Booker T. Washington
entries.subtitle: Educator and the most influential Black leader of his generation

cards.a: Educator and the most influential Black leader of his generation. Founding principal of Tuskegee Institute; Educator and orator; Political adviser

cards.q: When did Booker T. Washington live?
cards.a: Born 1856, Burroughs farm, Franklin County, Virginia; died November 14, 1915, Tuskegee, Alabama

cards.q: Who is this? Educator and the most influential Black leader of his generation
cards.a: Booker T. Washington
1856, enslaved on the Burroughs farm in Franklin County, Virginia
Opened July 4, 1881, with 30 students
September 18, 1895
First African American invited to dine at the White House (1901)

cards.q: Why does Booker T. Washington matter?
cards.a: Washington built one of the most important Black institutions in the country and defined one side of a lasting debate over how Black Americans should pursue freedom in the age of Jim Crow.

cards.q: What shaped Booker T. Washington early in life?
cards.a: Washington was born in 1856 on the Burroughs farm in Franklin County, Virginia, the son of the farm’s enslaved cook, Jane; he never knew the exact date or place, writing later only that “I suspect I must have been born somewhere and at some time.”

cards.q: What were Booker T. Washington’s major achievements?
cards.a: In May 1881 Hampton’s founder, General Armstrong, received a telegram from the board of commissioners of the new Tuskegee State Normal School in Alabama: “Booker T. Washington will suit us … send him at once.”

entries.title: Cesar Chavez
entries.subtitle: Labor leader and co-founder of the United Farm Workers

cards.a: Labor leader and co-founder of the United Farm Workers. Organizer, Community Service Organization; Co-founder, National Farm Workers Association (1962); President, United Farm Workers
Born March 31, 1927, near Yuma, Arizona; died April 23, 1993, San Luis, Arizona

cards.q: Who is this? Labor leader and co-founder of the United Farm Workers
cards.a: Cesar Chavez
National Farm Workers Association (1962), later the United Farm Workers
Began September 1965
Chavez showed that the most marginalized workers in America could organize, and he made the farm workers’ cause a national movement for dignity and civil rights.

cards.q: What shaped Cesar Chavez early in life?
cards.a: Cesar Estrada Chavez was born on March 31, 1927, near Yuma, Arizona, and named for his grandfather Cesario. He learned about injustice early: his father agreed to clear eighty acres in exchange for the deed to forty more beside their adobe home, but the bargain was broken, and after a lawyer’s scheme the family lost the land.

cards.q: What were Cesar Chavez’s major achievements?
cards.a: When the CSO refused to concentrate on farmworkers, Chavez quit and in 1962 founded the National Farm Workers Association in Delano, California, with Dolores Huerta; his brother Richard designed its black Aztec eagle on a red flag. For three years he traveled from town to town, meeting workers in their homes.

entries.title: Donald Trump
entries.subtitle: Forty-fifth and forty-seventh president, the second ever elected to non-consecutive terms

cards.a: Forty-fifth and forty-seventh president, the second ever elected to non-consecutive terms. Real estate developer and businessman; Television personality (*The Apprentice*); Forty-fifth president (2017–2021); Forty-seventh president (2025– )
Born June 14, 1946, Queens, New York City

cards.q: Who is this? Forty-fifth and forty-seventh president, the second ever elected to non-consecutive terms
cards.a: Donald Trump
January 20, 2017 – January 20, 2021; second term began January 20, 2025; Republican
Won the Electoral College 304–227 while Hillary Clinton won 2.8 million more popular votes
Beat Kamala Harris 312–226 in the Electoral College and 49.9% to 48.4% in the popular vote
First president with no prior public office or military leadership; first impeached twice; first convicted of a felony
The second president elected to non-consecutive terms, and the first since the nineteenth century

Trump put populist nationalism — opposition to immigration and free trade and skepticism of foreign alliances — at the center of Republican politics, and he broke with long-standing norms, above all by refusing to concede the 2020 election.

cards.q: What shaped Donald Trump early in life?
cards.a: Donald John Trump was born on June 14, 1946, in the borough of Queens in New York City, the fourth of five children of Mary Anne MacLeod Trump and Fred Trump, a residential real estate developer.

cards.q: What were Donald Trump’s major achievements?
cards.a: Trump announced his candidacy on June 16, 2015, at Trump Tower in Manhattan, promising to “Make America Great Again,” to build a wall on the Mexican border, and to put “America First.”

entries.title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
entries.subtitle: Commander of the D-Day invasion and thirty-fourth president, who presided over the prosperous, anxious 1950s

cards.a: Commander of the D-Day invasion and thirty-fourth president, who presided over the prosperous, anxious 1950s. Supreme Allied Commander, D-Day invasion (1944); Army chief of staff (1945–1948); President of Columbia University; First Supreme Commander of NATO forces in Europe; Thirty-fourth president (1953–1961)

cards.q: When did Dwight D. Eisenhower live?
cards.a: Born October 14, 1890, Denison, Texas; died March 28, 1969

cards.q: Who is this? Commander of the D-Day invasion and thirty-fourth president, who presided over the prosperous, anxious 1950s
cards.a: Dwight D. Eisenhower
January 20, 1953 – January 20, 1961; Republican
Gave the order — “Okay, let’s go” — for the Normandy invasion of June 6, 1944
Launched in 1956: a 41,000-mile network, the largest public works program in U.S. history
1957: the first president since Reconstruction to send troops into the South to enforce federal law
Beware the “military-industrial complex” (January 1961)
Ranked 22nd by historians in 1962; 8th by 1994

cards.q: Why does Dwight D. Eisenhower matter?
cards.a: Eisenhower led the largest invasion in history and then, as president, accepted the New Deal, built the interstates, and kept the Cold War from turning hot. His caution on civil rights and his reliance on covert action left problems his successors had to face.

cards.q: What shaped Dwight D. Eisenhower early in life?
cards.a: Eisenhower was born on October 14, 1890, in a house by the railroad tracks in Denison, Texas, and grew up in the small farm town of Abilene, Kansas. His father worked as a mechanic in a creamery; his mother, Ida, a Mennonite, was a religious pacifist — though she did not try to stop her son from becoming a soldier.

cards.q: What were Dwight D. Eisenhower’s major achievements?
cards.a: Huge army maneuvers in Louisiana, with more than 400,000 troops, revealed his gift for strategic planning, and days after Pearl Harbor he was called to Washington to work on war plans. He so impressed the Army chief of staff, George C. Marshall, that promotions came quickly.

entries.title: Eleanor Roosevelt
entries.subtitle: First lady, reformer, and champion of human rights

cards.a: First lady, reformer, and champion of human rights. First Lady (1933–1945); Delegate to the United Nations; Chair of the UN Human Rights Commission; Chair of the President’s Commission on the Status of Women
Born October 11, 1884, New York City; died November 7, 1962

cards.q: Who is this? First lady, reformer, and champion of human rights
cards.a: Eleanor Roosevelt
Franklin D. Roosevelt, a fifth cousin once removed, on March 17, 1905
Chaired the Human Rights Commission; Universal Declaration adopted December 10, 1948
Eleanor Roosevelt used an unelected position to become one of the most influential reformers of the twentieth century and a founding voice of the international human rights movement.

cards.q: What shaped Eleanor Roosevelt early in life?
cards.a: Anna Eleanor Roosevelt was born on October 11, 1884, in New York City, the niece of Theodore Roosevelt. Her privileged childhood was also a sad one: her father struggled with alcoholism, and by the time she was ten her mother, her father, and a brother had died.

cards.q: What were Eleanor Roosevelt’s major achievements?
cards.a: Her public life began in earnest during World War I, when she volunteered with the Red Cross and in Navy hospitals.

entries.title: Elizabeth Cady Stanton
entries.subtitle: Philosopher and strategist of the women’s rights movement

cards.a: Philosopher and strategist of the women’s rights movement. Organizer of the Seneca Falls Convention; Author of the Declaration of Sentiments; President of the National Woman Suffrage Association; Author of *The Woman’s Bible*

cards.q: When did Elizabeth Cady Stanton live?
cards.a: Born November 12, 1815, Johnstown, New York; died October 1902, New York City

cards.q: Who is this? Philosopher and strategist of the women’s rights movement
cards.a: Elizabeth Cady Stanton
With Susan B. Anthony, from 1851, for more than fifty years
Co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association (1869)
Declaration of Sentiments (1848); History of Woman Suffrage; The Woman’s Bible
1902 — eighteen years before women of her social status could vote nationally

cards.q: Why does Elizabeth Cady Stanton matter?
cards.a: Stanton gave the women’s movement its ideas and much of its language. Her career also shows the movement’s internal conflicts over race, which shaped suffrage politics for decades.

cards.q: What shaped Elizabeth Cady Stanton early in life?
cards.a: Elizabeth Cady was born on November 12, 1815, in Johnstown, New York, the eighth of ten children of Margaret Livingston and Daniel Cady, a lawyer who became a state supreme court judge. Four of his five sons died in infancy, and the fifth when Elizabeth was eleven.

cards.q: What were Elizabeth Cady Stanton’s major achievements?
cards.a: In London, Stanton and the Quaker abolitionist Lucretia Mott were furious that women were barred from speaking, and they resolved to hold a convention on women’s rights. In 1848 they did so at Seneca Falls, New York.

entries.title: Elvis Presley
entries.subtitle: The “King of Rock & Roll,” who carried a blend of Black and white Southern music to a mass audience

cards.a: The “King of Rock & Roll,” who carried a blend of Black and white Southern music to a mass audience. Singer; Film actor; U.S. Army soldier (1958–1960)
Born January 8, 1935, Tupelo, Mississippi; died August 16, 1977, Graceland, Memphis, Tennessee

cards.q: Who is this? The “King of Rock & Roll,” who carried a blend of Black and white Southern music to a mass audience
cards.a: Elvis Presley
“That’s All Right” (1954), a blues song by Arthur Crudup, recorded for Sam Phillips’s Sun Records
“Heartbreak Hotel” (1956), his first single for RCA Victor and his first number-one hit
Drafted in 1958 at the height of his fame; served in Germany; honorably discharged in March 1960
First film, Love Me Tender (1956); for most of the 1960s he concentrated on making movies
Inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1986

Presley was the figure through whom rock & roll exploded into mainstream culture. By bringing Black-influenced music to white audiences in the segregated 1950s, he helped remake American popular music and youth culture.

cards.q: What shaped Elvis Presley early in life?
cards.a: Elvis Aron Presley was born on January 8, 1935, in a two-room house in Tupelo, Mississippi, to Vernon and Gladys Presley. His twin brother, Jessie Garon, was stillborn, so Elvis grew up an only child.

cards.q: What were Elvis Presley’s major achievements?
cards.a: In 1953 and 1954 Presley cut demo records at Sun Records, whose owner, Sam Phillips, had been looking for a white singer who could perform in the style of traditionally Black music.

entries.title: Federalism
