entries.subtitle: How power is divided between the national government and the states

cards.a: How power is divided between the national government and the states

cards.q: Name it: How power is divided between the national government and the states
cards.a: Federalism
Enumerated powers (Article I), the supremacy clause (Article VI), and the Tenth Amendment
The Articles of Confederation left the states almost fully sovereign
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Civil War and Reconstruction amendments, the New Deal, the civil rights era

Federalism shapes almost every American political fight, because the question “Which government should decide?” is often as contested as the decision itself. Appeals to states’ rights have defended both local self-government and, at times, slavery and segregation.
In a federal system, two levels of government each have real authority over the same people.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: The framers devised federalism as a middle path between the weak league of the Articles of Confederation and a single centralized government. Madison argued that dividing power between two levels, as well as among branches, would give citizens a “double security” for their rights.

entries.title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
entries.subtitle: Thirty-second president, architect of the New Deal and wartime leader

cards.a: Thirty-second president, architect of the New Deal and wartime leader. New York state senator (1911–1913); Assistant Secretary of the Navy (1913–1920); Democratic vice-presidential nominee (1920); Governor of New York (1929–1932); Thirty-second president (1933–1945)

cards.q: When did Franklin D. Roosevelt live?
cards.a: Born January 30, 1882, Hyde Park, New York; died April 12, 1945, Warm Springs, Georgia

cards.q: Who is this? Thirty-second president, architect of the New Deal and wartime leader
cards.a: Franklin D. Roosevelt
Eleanor Roosevelt, a distant cousin and the niece of Theodore Roosevelt, married in 1905
Struck in the summer of 1921 at Campobello Island; never regained the use of his legs
1933–1945; Democrat; elected 1932, 1936, 1940, and 1944, the only president to serve more than two terms
The New Deal: banking reform, CCC, WPA, TVA, Social Security, the Wagner Act
Lend-Lease (March 1941); led the nation after Pearl Harbor (December 7, 1941)

cards.q: Why does Franklin D. Roosevelt matter?
cards.a: Roosevelt changed what Americans expected from their government and their president. Under him the federal government took responsibility for the economic security of ordinary citizens, the Democratic Party became the nation’s majority party, and the United States emerged from World War II as a global power.

cards.q: What shaped Franklin D. Roosevelt early in life?
cards.a: Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born on January 30, 1882, at Hyde Park, New York, the only child of James Roosevelt, a wealthy landowner and businessman, and Sara Delano Roosevelt, who devoted herself to her son throughout her long life. He grew up on the family estate on the Hudson River, taught by tutors until he was fourteen, when he entered the Groton School.

cards.q: What were Franklin D. Roosevelt’s major achievements?
cards.a: Election and the New Deal. At the 1932 Democratic convention in Chicago, Roosevelt broke with tradition by flying there to accept the nomination in person.

entries.title: Frederick Douglass
entries.subtitle: Escaped slave, orator, editor, and the foremost Black leader of the nineteenth century

cards.a: Escaped slave, orator, editor, and the foremost Black leader of the nineteenth century. Abolitionist lecturer and author; Editor of *The North Star*; Recruiter of Black Union soldiers; President of the Freedman’s Bank (1874); U.S. Marshal for D.C. (1877–1881); Recorder of Deeds for D.C. (1881–1886); Minister Resident and Consul General to Haiti (1889–1891)
Born February 1818, Talbot County, Eastern Shore of Maryland; died February 20, 1895, Cedar Hill, Washington, D.C.

cards.q: Who is this? Escaped slave, orator, editor, and the foremost Black leader of the nineteenth century
cards.a: Frederick Douglass
February 1818, Talbot County, Maryland; he later chose February 14 as his birthday
September 3, 1838, from Baltimore to New York, by train and boat, dressed as a sailor
Narrative (1845), My Bondage and My Freedom (1855), Life and Times (1881)
The North Star, first issue December 3, 1847, Rochester, New York
1846, for £150 raised by British supporters
U.S. Marshal and Recorder of Deeds for D.C.; minister to Haiti (1889–1891)

Douglass turned his own life into the most powerful argument against slavery that Americans ever heard, and then spent thirty years after emancipation insisting that freedom meant nothing without citizenship, the vote, and equal rights. He judged the nation by its own founding words, and he believed in building alliances across racial and political lines to make them true.

cards.q: What shaped Frederick Douglass early in life?
cards.a: Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey was born into slavery on the Eastern Shore of Maryland in February 1818. He barely knew his mother, who was forced to work on a distant farm and died when he was about seven, and he never knew his father.

cards.q: What were Frederick Douglass’s major achievements?
cards.a: Abolitionist. In August 1841, at an antislavery convention on Nantucket, Douglass spoke to a large, mostly white audience, and the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society hired him as a lecturer. He toured the North and Midwest.

entries.title: George Washington
entries.subtitle: Commander of the Continental Army and first president

cards.a: Commander of the Continental Army and first president. Virginia militia officer in the French and Indian War; Member of the Virginia House of Burgesses (from 1759); Commander in chief of the Continental Army (1775–1783); President of the Constitutional Convention (1787); First president of the United States (1789–1797)
Born February 22, 1732, Westmoreland County, Virginia; died December 14, 1799, Mount Vernon, Virginia

cards.q: Who is this? Commander of the Continental Army and first president
cards.a: George Washington
February 22, 1732 (February 11 by the old calendar), at Popes Creek, Westmoreland County, Virginia
Elected by Congress in June 1775; resigned his commission to Congress in December 1783
Unanimously by the Electoral College in 1789 (69 votes) and 1792 (132 votes), the only president elected unanimously twice
Created the cabinet; retired after two terms, a limit later written into the 22nd Amendment
His will freed the people he held in his own right, after Martha Washington’s death
December 14, 1799, at Mount Vernon, of an acute throat infection

Washington’s greatest contribution was his restraint. Americans trusted him with immense power because he had given it up once before, and his conduct as president created the cabinet, the two-term tradition, and the dignity of the office. His slaveholding is the most troubling part of his legacy.

cards.q: What shaped George Washington early in life?
cards.a: Washington was born on February 22, 1732, at Popes Creek farm in Westmoreland County, Virginia.

cards.q: What were George Washington’s major achievements?
cards.a: Commander in chief. Washington attended the Second Continental Congress in uniform.

entries.title: Harpers Ferry
entries.subtitle: Armory town where John Brown struck at slavery

cards.a: Armory town where John Brown struck at slavery
Harpers Ferry, West Virginia, where the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers meet · South

cards.q: Name it: Armory town where John Brown struck at slavery
cards.a: Harpers Ferry
First successful application of interchangeable manufacture, at the U.S. armory
October 16–18, 1859
Site of the largest surrender of Federal troops during the war
Harpers Ferry National Historical Park

Harpers Ferry concentrates several stories of nineteenth-century America in one small town: industrial innovation, the violent struggle over slavery, the Civil War, and the beginnings of Black education after emancipation.

The town sits on steep ground at the junction of the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers. Its preserved nineteenth-century streets and buildings are part of Harpers Ferry National Historical Park, which also studies the area’s archeological record going back millennia.

The National Park Service describes Harpers Ferry’s history as multilayered. The U.S. armory there pioneered interchangeable manufacture, and the town was reached by one of the first successful American railroads.

entries.title: Harriet Tubman
entries.subtitle: Freedom seeker, Underground Railroad conductor, Union scout

cards.a: Freedom seeker, Underground Railroad conductor, Union scout. Underground Railroad conductor; Union Army scout, spy, and nurse; Leader in the Combahee River Raid; Women’s suffrage advocate
Born c. 1822, Dorchester County, Eastern Shore of Maryland; died March 10, 1913, Auburn, New York

cards.q: Who is this? Freedom seeker, Underground Railroad conductor, Union scout
cards.a: Harriet Tubman
About 1822, Dorchester County, Maryland, named Araminta (“Minty”) Ross
Fall 1849, after her enslaver died and she feared being sold
About 13 trips to Maryland between 1850 and 1860, guiding some 70 people to freedom
June 1–2, 1863: more than 700 people freed (most National Park Service accounts say over 750)
“Moses”; John Brown called her “General Tubman”
March 10, 1913, in Auburn, New York
Tubman turned her own escape into a lifelong campaign against slavery, risking recapture again and again to free others.

cards.q: What shaped Harriet Tubman early in life?
cards.a: Harriet Tubman was born Araminta Ross around 1822 in Dorchester County, on the Eastern Shore of Maryland, one of nine children of Harriet “Rit” Green Ross and Benjamin Ross. Under slavery the children of an enslaved mother were enslaved too, whatever their father’s status; Ben Ross was free, but Rit and her children were held by a man named Edward Brodess. Brodess broke the family apart.

cards.q: What were Harriet Tubman’s major achievements?
cards.a: In March 1849 Edward Brodess died.

entries.title: Harry S. Truman
entries.subtitle: Thirty-third president: ended World War II and launched the Cold War containment policy

cards.a: Thirty-third president: ended World War II and launched the Cold War containment policy. Presiding judge, Jackson County, Missouri; U.S. Senator from Missouri (elected 1934); Vice President (1945); Thirty-third president (1945–1953)

cards.q: When did Harry S. Truman live?
cards.a: Born May 8, 1884, Lamar, Missouri; died December 26, 1972

cards.q: Who is this? Thirty-third president: ended World War II and launched the Cold War containment policy
cards.a: Harry S. Truman
April 12, 1945 – January 1953; Democrat
Truman Doctrine (1947), Marshall Plan, Berlin Airlift, NATO (1949), Korean War
Executive Order 9981 (1948) desegregated the armed forces
Upset victory over Thomas Dewey

cards.q: Why does Harry S. Truman matter?
cards.a: Truman made the decisions that ended World War II and set the course of American foreign policy for the next four decades.

cards.q: What shaped Harry S. Truman early in life?
cards.a: Truman was born on May 8, 1884, in Lamar, Missouri, and grew up in Independence, a small town with Southern ways on the old trails to the West. Born with poor eyesight and kept by his mother from rough games, he became a passionate reader of history and a fine pianist who briefly considered a concert career.

cards.q: What were Harry S. Truman’s major achievements?
cards.a: In 1922 Tom Pendergast, Kansas City’s Democratic boss, backed Truman for county judge, an administrative post. As presiding judge from 1926 he rebuilt Jackson County’s roads and managed its finances in the early Depression, earning a reputation for honesty inside a corrupt machine.

entries.title: Henry Ford
entries.subtitle: Automaker who put America on wheels with the Model T, the moving assembly line, and the Five Dollar Day

cards.a: Automaker who put America on wheels with the Model T, the moving assembly line, and the Five Dollar Day. Engineer, Edison Electric Illuminating Company; Founder of Ford Motor Company (1903); Owner of *The Dearborn Independent*
Born July 30, 1863, Dearborn, Michigan; died 1947

cards.q: Who is this? Automaker who put America on wheels with the Model T, the moving assembly line, and the Five Dollar Day
cards.a: Henry Ford
Founded June 16, 1903, after two failed car companies
Introduced October 1, 1908; about 15 million sold before production ended in 1927
1913: chassis assembly time cut from 12.5 hours to 1.5
January 1914: double the going factory wage, for an eight-hour day
Antisemitic series in his Dearborn Independent, 1920–1922

Ford’s methods of mass production and mass consumption — standardized products, assembly lines, and high wages that let workers buy what they made — became a model for twentieth-century industry. His career also shows how fame and wealth could amplify hatred: his antisemitic publications circulated worldwide for decades.

cards.q: What shaped Henry Ford early in life?
cards.a: Henry Ford was born on July 30, 1863, on a farm in what is now Dearborn, Michigan. As a boy he showed a gift for machinery, a talent for leadership, and a preference for learning by trial and error.

cards.q: What were Henry Ford’s major achievements?
cards.a: Ford’s first two car companies failed. In 1901 his racing car beat the era’s top driver, and on June 16, 1903, a new group of investors founded the Ford Motor Company; its first Model A sold on July 23, and by October the company had turned a profit.

entries.title: Ida B. Wells
entries.subtitle: Journalist who exposed lynching and fought for civil rights and suffrage

cards.a: Journalist who exposed lynching and fought for civil rights and suffrage. Teacher; Journalist and newspaper owner (“Iola”); Anti-lynching crusader; Suffragist and founder of the Alpha Suffrage Club; Co-founder of Black women’s organizations and an organizer of the NAACP

cards.q: When did Ida B. Wells live?
cards.a: Born July 16, 1862, Holly Springs, Mississippi; died March 1931, Chicago, Illinois

cards.q: Who is this? Journalist who exposed lynching and fought for civil rights and suffrage
cards.a: Ida B. Wells
July 16, 1862, Holly Springs, Mississippi, enslaved
Forcibly removed from a first-class car in May 1884; won in a lower court, lost on appeal to the Tennessee Supreme Court
Co-owner and editor of the Memphis Free Speech, destroyed by a mob in 1892
Southern Horrors (1892), The Reason Why (1893), A Red Record (1895)
Founded the Alpha Suffrage Club in Chicago, January 30, 1913
March 1931, Chicago (sources give March 15 and March 25)

cards.q: Why does Ida B. Wells matter?
cards.a: Wells used investigative journalism, statistics, and the reports of white newspapers themselves to expose lynching and the excuses made for it. She linked the fight against racial violence to the fight for women’s votes, and her career shows how Black women shaped both the civil rights and suffrage movements.

cards.q: What shaped Ida B. Wells early in life?
cards.a: Ida Bell Wells was born enslaved in Holly Springs, Mississippi, on July 16, 1862, the oldest daughter of James and Elizabeth (Lizzie) Wells. She and her parents were freed at the end of the Civil War. During Reconstruction her parents were active in the Republican Party, and her father helped found Rust College, a historically Black college, where she studied. In the fall of 1878 yellow fever killed both of her parents and one of her siblings.

cards.q: What were Ida B. Wells’s major achievements?
cards.a: The Memphis lynching. In 1892 a white mob lynched Thomas Moss, Calvin McDowell, and a third man (the National Park Service names him Will Stewart, the National Women’s History Museum Henry Steward). They owned the People’s Grocery, which had drawn customers from a white-owned store.

entries.title: Independence Hall
entries.subtitle: Where the Declaration and the Constitution were debated and signed

cards.a: Where the Declaration and the Constitution were debated and signed
Chestnut Street, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania · Northeast

cards.q: Name it: Where the Declaration and the Constitution were debated and signed
cards.a: Independence Hall
Pennsylvania State House, home to the colony’s three branches of government
Washington named commander in chief (1775); Declaration adopted (1776); Articles of Confederation took effect (1781); Constitution written (1787)
National Park Service, Independence National Historical Park
Few buildings anywhere have hosted as many foundational political acts. Independence Hall is the physical center of the American founding.

Independence Hall is a Georgian-style brick building on Chestnut Street in Philadelphia. Its Assembly Room, where the Pennsylvania legislature met, was lent to the Second Continental Congress and later to the Constitutional Convention.
Construction began in 1732 on a building to house all three branches of Pennsylvania’s colonial government.

entries.title: Jackie Robinson
entries.subtitle: The ballplayer who broke baseball’s color barrier in 1947, and a civil rights advocate

cards.a: The ballplayer who broke baseball’s color barrier in 1947, and a civil rights advocate. Kansas City Monarchs, Negro Leagues (1945); Brooklyn Dodgers (1947–1956); Civil rights advocate
Born January 31, 1919, Cairo, Georgia; died October 24, 1972, Stamford, Connecticut

cards.q: Who is this? The ballplayer who broke baseball’s color barrier in 1947, and a civil rights advocate
cards.a: Jackie Robinson
April 15, 1947, Brooklyn Dodgers
Rookie of the Year (1947); National League MVP (1949); Hall of Fame (1962)
.313 batting average, 1,563 hits, 200 stolen bases
Six pennants in his ten seasons and the 1955 World Series title
Every major league team celebrates Jackie Robinson Day on April 15
Robinson integrated the national pastime in 1947, showing millions of Americans what equal opportunity could look like — and then used his fame to press for civil rights.

cards.q: What shaped Jackie Robinson early in life?
cards.a: Jack Roosevelt Robinson was born on January 31, 1919, in Cairo, Georgia, the youngest of five children of sharecroppers Jerry and Mallie Robinson. His father left the family when Jackie was an infant, and in 1920 his mother moved the children by train to Pasadena, California, where she worked as a domestic.

cards.q: What were Jackie Robinson’s major achievements?
cards.a: Brooklyn Dodgers president Branch Rickey chose Robinson to break baseball’s unwritten color line — for his talent, but also because he was college-educated, had competed with and against white athletes, and could stand the spotlight.

entries.title: James Madison
entries.subtitle: Architect of the Constitution and fourth president

cards.a: Architect of the Constitution and fourth president. Member of the Continental Congress; Delegate to the Constitutional Convention; Co-author of the Federalist Papers; U.S. representative who drafted the Bill of Rights; Secretary of state (1801–1809); Fourth president (1809–1817); Rector of the University of Virginia
Born March 16, 1751, Port Conway, Virginia; died June 28, 1836, Montpelier, Virginia

cards.q: Who is this? Architect of the Constitution and fourth president
cards.a: James Madison
March 16, 1751, at Belle Grove plantation, Port Conway, King George County, Virginia
College of New Jersey (Princeton), 1769–1771
Author of the Virginia Plan (1787); wrote 29 Federalist essays; proposed the amendments that became the Bill of Rights
Co-founder, with Jefferson, of the Republican (Democratic-Republican) Party
1809–1817; elected 1808 (122 electoral votes to 47) and 1812 (128 to 89)
Signed the declaration of war June 18, 1812; British troops burned Washington in August 1814
Madison’s ideas about large republics, factions, and checks and balances, set out in the Federalist Papers, remain central to American constitutional thought.

cards.q: What shaped James Madison early in life?
cards.a: James Madison was born on March 16, 1751, at Belle Grove, his mother’s family plantation at Port Conway in King George County, Virginia.

cards.q: What were James Madison’s major achievements?
cards.a: The Constitution. Madison studied the failures of earlier confederacies and concluded that the United States needed a strong national republic. His Virginia Plan, adopted in May 1787 as the Convention’s agenda, proposed three branches of government and a two-house legislature based on population. He won on representation by population in the House and on separate executive and judicial branches, but he lost on equal representation in the Senate and on a congressional veto over state laws, and for a time he doubted the new government could succeed. Throughout the Convention he kept detailed notes of the debates.

entries.title: Jazz
entries.subtitle: America’s homegrown music, born in New Orleans

cards.a: America’s homegrown music, born in New Orleans

cards.q: Name it: America’s homegrown music, born in New Orleans
cards.a: Jazz
New Orleans, Louisiana
Cornetist Charles “Buddy” Bolden, 1895–1900
Cornet, clarinet, and trombone, improvising together
1917, by the Original Dixieland Jazz Band in New York
Riverboats, touring shows, records, and radio
Jazz is one of the clearest examples of how African American culture shaped the whole nation’s — it gave the 1920s their name and became one of America’s best-known contributions to world music.
Jazz, in the words of The American Yawp, is “a uniquely American musical style” popularized by the African American community in New Orleans.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: New Orleans had a culture unlike the rest of the young United States: Catholic and French-speaking, fond of festivals and dancing, and shaped by Africans and people of African descent, who made up more than half the city’s population by the end of the 1700s.

entries.title: Jim Crow
entries.subtitle: The system of legal segregation and disenfranchisement, 1880s–1960s

cards.a: The system of legal segregation and disenfranchisement, 1880s–1960s

cards.q: Name it: The system of legal segregation and disenfranchisement, 1880s–1960s
cards.a: Jim Crow
From a Black character in minstrel shows
From the 1880s into the 1960s
Plessy v. Ferguson (May 18, 1896), “equal but separate accommodations”
Poll taxes, literacy tests, and “grandfather clauses,” adopted mostly from about 1890 to 1908
White mobs killed roughly 5,000 African Americans between the 1880s and the 1950s
Brown v. Board (1954), the Civil Rights Act (1964), and the Voting Rights Act (1965)
Jim Crow made a mockery of the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments for most of a century.

Jim Crow was a system of white supremacy built on three foundations: segregation, disenfranchisement, and violence. Segregation laws separated Black and white Americans in public life, from schools and trains to restaurants, theaters, restrooms, hospitals, and graveyards, and banned marriage between the races, punishing violators under the law. Disenfranchisement laws used poll taxes, literacy tests, and other devices to keep Black men from voting despite the Fifteenth Amendment. And lynching and mob violence punished anyone who challenged the order. The name came from “Jim Crow,” a Black character in minstrel shows. Although Jim Crow is most associated with the South, the National Park Service notes that a majority of states, from Delaware to California and from North Dakota to Texas, had such laws at some point.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: The end of Reconstruction. When federal troops withdrew from the South in 1877, white Democrats who called themselves “Redeemers” regained power across the region, and the number of Black officeholders declined significantly. At first segregation was often a matter of custom.

entries.title: Joe Biden
entries.subtitle: Forty-sixth president, after thirty-six years in the Senate and eight as vice president

cards.a: Forty-sixth president, after thirty-six years in the Senate and eight as vice president. U.S. Senator from Delaware (1973–2009); Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee; Vice president under Barack Obama (2009–2017); Forty-sixth president (2021–2025)
Born November 20, 1942, Scranton, Pennsylvania

cards.q: Who is this? Forty-sixth president, after thirty-six years in the Senate and eight as vice president
cards.a: Joe Biden
January 20, 2021 – January 20, 2025; Democrat
306 electoral votes to Trump’s 232; about 81 million popular votes, 7 million more than Trump
American Rescue Plan (2021), Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (2021), CHIPS and Science Act and Inflation Reduction Act (2022), Respect for Marriage Act (2022)
Appointed Ketanji Brown Jackson, the first Black woman on the Court (2022)
“Amtrak Joe,” for decades of daily train commutes between Wilmington and Washington

Biden’s long career spanned the Senate of the 1970s to the polarized politics of the 2020s. His presidency combined major new federal investments with an effort to rebuild alliances after the Trump years; its record on the pandemic, inflation, immigration, and foreign wars remains a subject of debate.

cards.q: What shaped Joe Biden early in life?
cards.a: Joseph Robinette Biden Jr. was born on November 20, 1942, in Scranton, Pennsylvania, the oldest child of a working-class Irish Catholic family. When his father’s business fortunes collapsed after World War II, Joe Sr. took whatever work he could find; in 1953 he found a job selling cars and moved the family to Delaware.

cards.q: What were Joe Biden’s major achievements?
cards.a: In the Senate Biden became a leading figure on the Judiciary and Foreign Relations Committees and chaired the confirmation hearings of five Supreme Court justices, including the bitterly contested nominations of Robert Bork and Clarence Thomas.

entries.title: John Adams
entries.subtitle: Revolutionary leader, diplomat, and second president, who kept the young nation out of war with France

cards.a: Revolutionary leader, diplomat, and second president, who kept the young nation out of war with France. Lawyer; Delegate to the Continental Congress (1774–1777); Diplomat in Europe (1778–1788); First U.S. minister to Great Britain (1785); First vice president (1789–1797); Second president (1797–1801)
Born October 30, 1735, Braintree (now Quincy), Massachusetts; died July 4, 1826, Quincy, Massachusetts

cards.q: Who is this? Revolutionary leader, diplomat, and second president, who kept the young nation out of war with France
cards.a: John Adams
March 4, 1797 – March 4, 1801; Federalist
Defended the British soldiers in 1770; none was sent to jail
Nominated George Washington to command the Continental Army; served on about ninety committees and chaired twenty
Beat Jefferson 71 electoral votes to 68 — and got Jefferson, from the rival party, as his vice president
“Thomas Jefferson survives” — Jefferson had died hours earlier, on July 4, 1826, the Declaration’s fiftieth anniversary
Husband of Abigail Adams; father of John Quincy Adams, the sixth president

Adams helped drive the colonies to independence and shaped American constitutional thinking about separated powers and a strong executive. As president he kept the fragile republic out of a full-scale war with France — but the Sedition Act he signed showed how easily a government could turn on its critics.

cards.q: What shaped John Adams early in life?
cards.a: Adams was born on October 30, 1735, in Braintree (now Quincy), Massachusetts, into a comfortable but not wealthy farming family; his father was a farmer, shoemaker, and church deacon who hoped his son would become a minister.

cards.q: What were John Adams’s major achievements?
cards.a: Adams went to the First Continental Congress in 1774 and soon led the faction pushing for independence.

entries.title: John Brown
entries.subtitle: Abolitionist who led the 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry

cards.a: Abolitionist who led the 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry. Abolitionist; Tanner, farmer, and wool merchant; Antislavery fighter in Kansas; Leader of the raid on Harpers Ferry
Born May 9, 1800, Torrington, Connecticut; died December 2, 1859, Charles Town, Virginia (now West Virginia)

cards.q: Who is this? Abolitionist who led the 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry
cards.a: John Brown
October 16–18, 1859, with 21 followers
U.S. Marines commanded by Colonel Robert E. Lee
December 2, 1859, in Charles Town, Virginia
John Brown’s raid convinced many Southerners that the North would not leave slavery alone, and many Northerners that slavery could not be ended peacefully — pushing the nation closer to civil war.

cards.q: What shaped John Brown early in life?
cards.a: Brown was born on May 9, 1800, in Torrington, Connecticut, and grew up in Hudson, Ohio. As a boy he saw an enslaved boy he had befriended savagely beaten — a sight that, with his conviction that slavery was a sin against God, shaped the rest of his life.

cards.q: What were John Brown’s major achievements?
cards.a: When the Kansas-Nebraska Act turned Kansas into a battleground over slavery, Brown followed members of his family there to “strike a blow for freedom.”

entries.title: John F. Kennedy
entries.subtitle: Thirty-fifth president: the youngest ever elected, assassinated in Dallas in 1963

cards.a: Thirty-fifth president: the youngest ever elected, assassinated in Dallas in 1963. U.S. Navy officer in World War II; U.S. Representative from Massachusetts (1947–1953); U.S. Senator from Massachusetts (1953–1960); Thirty-fifth president (1961–1963)

cards.q: When did John F. Kennedy live?
cards.a: Born May 29, 1917, Brookline, Massachusetts; died November 22, 1963, Dallas, Texas

cards.q: Who is this? Thirty-fifth president: the youngest ever elected, assassinated in Dallas in 1963
cards.a: John F. Kennedy
January 20, 1961 – November 22, 1963; Democrat
Beat Richard Nixon by fewer than 120,000 votes out of 68.8 million; 303 electoral votes to 219
Youngest person elected president; first Roman Catholic president; first president born in the twentieth century
After a Japanese destroyer rammed his boat, PT 109, in 1943, he towed a burned crewman to safety by a strap held in his teeth
Profiles in Courage won the Pulitzer Prize for biography in 1957
November 22, 1963, in Dallas; the Warren Commission found that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone

cards.q: Why does John F. Kennedy matter?
cards.a: Kennedy's presidency brought the Cold War to its most dangerous moment and then to a first step back from it, the 1963 test ban treaty. His youth, eloquence, and command of television changed American politics, and his murder left a lasting sense of what might have been.

cards.q: What shaped John F. Kennedy early in life?
cards.a: John Fitzgerald Kennedy was born on May 29, 1917, in Brookline, Massachusetts, into a rich, politically connected family of Irish Catholics; his maternal grandfather had been mayor of Boston, and his father, Joseph P. Kennedy, had made a fortune in the stock market and entertainment and pulled his money out just before the crash of 1929.

cards.q: What were John F. Kennedy’s major achievements?
cards.a: In 1960 Kennedy won the Democratic nomination by beating Hubert Humphrey in the primaries — above all in heavily Protestant West Virginia, where he had to prove a wealthy Catholic could win.

entries.title: John Marshall
entries.subtitle: Fourth Chief Justice, who made the Supreme Court a co-equal branch

cards.a: Fourth Chief Justice, who made the Supreme Court a co-equal branch. Continental Army officer; Virginia lawyer and legislator; U.S. representative (1799–1800); Secretary of state (1800–1801); Chief Justice of the United States (1801–1835)
Born September 24, 1755, Prince William (later Fauquier) County, Virginia; died July 6, 1835, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

cards.q: Who is this? Fourth Chief Justice, who made the Supreme Court a co-equal branch
cards.a: John Marshall
By President John Adams; confirmed January 27, 1801
1801–1835, the longest tenure of any Chief Justice
Marbury v. Madison (1803), McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), Gibbons v. Ogden (1824), Worcester v. Georgia (1832)
College of William and Mary, 1780
More than any founder, Marshall defined what the Constitution would mean in practice — and made the Supreme Court the institution that says what the law is.

cards.q: What shaped John Marshall early in life?
cards.a: Marshall was born on September 24, 1755, in Prince William (now Fauquier) County, Virginia, and grew up on his father’s estate, Oak Hill. At a local academy he befriended a future president, James Monroe.

cards.q: What were John Marshall’s major achievements?
cards.a: A Federalist, Marshall was a delegate to Virginia’s 1788 convention that ratified the Constitution.

entries.title: Little Rock Central High School
entries.subtitle: Site of the 1957 desegregation crisis, now a National Historic Site

cards.q: What is Little Rock Central High School?
cards.a: Site of the 1957 desegregation crisis, now a National Historic Site
Little Rock, Arkansas · South

cards.q: Name it: Site of the 1957 desegregation crisis, now a National Historic Site
cards.a: Little Rock Central High School
Construction began 1926, as Little Rock Senior High School
About 1,800 students in grades 10–12
An operating four-year public high school of about 2,500 students
Little Rock Central High School National Historic Site (National Park Service)
2120 W. Daisy L. Gatson Bates Drive

cards.q: Why does Little Rock Central High School matter?
cards.a: Central High is a landmark of the civil rights movement — a place where the federal government enforced the Constitution against a state’s resistance.

Central High is an active school, so public access inside the building is limited; National Park Service rangers lead guided tours of the grounds. The street in front of the visitor center is named for Daisy Bates, the NAACP leader who guided the nine students.
Construction of Little Rock Senior High School, later renamed Central High, began in 1926.

entries.title: Louis Armstrong
entries.subtitle: New Orleans trumpeter and singer who made jazz a soloist’s art and a world music

cards.a: New Orleans trumpeter and singer who made jazz a soloist’s art and a world music. Cornetist and trumpeter; Singer and bandleader; Film performer; Unofficial goodwill ambassador abroad
Born August 4, 1901, New Orleans, Louisiana; died July 6, 1971, Corona, Queens, New York

cards.q: Who is this? New Orleans trumpeter and singer who made jazz a soloist’s art and a world music
cards.a: Louis Armstrong
“Satchmo”; abroad, “Ambassador Satch”
Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings, 1925–1928
“Heebie Jeebies” (1926), “Hello, Dolly!” (1964), “What a Wonderful World” (1968)
First African American to host a sponsored national radio broadcast (1937); first jazz musician on the cover of Time (1949)
August 4, 1901 — though he often claimed July 4, 1900
Armstrong turned jazz into an art of individual improvisation and carried it around the world, making a music born in Black New Orleans one of America’s best-known cultural exports.

cards.q: What shaped Louis Armstrong early in life?
cards.a: Armstrong was born on August 4, 1901, in New Orleans — though for most of his life he claimed July 4, 1900.

cards.q: What were Louis Armstrong’s major achievements?
cards.a: In 1922 Oliver sent for Armstrong to join his Creole Jazz Band in Chicago, where their intricate two-cornet breaks became the talk of the town; they began recording in 1923. Armstrong married the band’s pianist, Lil Hardin, in 1924, and she urged him to strike out on his own.

entries.title: Lyndon B. Johnson
entries.subtitle: Thirty-sixth president: the Great Society, civil rights, and Vietnam

cards.a: Thirty-sixth president: the Great Society, civil rights, and Vietnam. U.S. Representative from Texas (1937–1949); U.S. Senator and Senate Majority Leader; Vice President (1961–1963); Thirty-sixth president (1963–1969)

cards.q: When did Lyndon B. Johnson live?
cards.a: Born August 27, 1908, Texas Hill Country; died January 22, 1973

cards.q: Who is this? Thirty-sixth president: the Great Society, civil rights, and Vietnam
cards.a: Lyndon B. Johnson
August 27, 1908, in the Texas Hill Country
November 22, 1963 – January 1969; Democrat
Won 61.1% of the popular vote against Barry Goldwater
Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts, Medicare and Medicaid, War on Poverty, immigration reform
U.S. troops rose to almost 200,000 by the end of 1965 and more than 500,000 within three years

cards.q: Why does Lyndon B. Johnson matter?
cards.a: Johnson enacted the most sweeping domestic reforms since the New Deal, while his Vietnam policy tore the country apart.

cards.q: What shaped Lyndon B. Johnson early in life?
cards.a: Johnson was born on August 27, 1908, in a farmhouse on the Pedernales River, the first of five children; his father, a state legislator, rode up and down the river announcing that his son would be governor of Texas someday. Their house in Johnson City had neither electricity nor indoor plumbing.

cards.q: What were Lyndon B. Johnson’s major achievements?
cards.a: Appointed Texas director of the New Deal’s National Youth Administration in 1935, Johnson helped young people stay in school and find work. In 1937, at twenty-eight, he won a seat in Congress as a Roosevelt ally and brought electricity to the Hill Country of his youth — the achievement he called his proudest.

entries.title: Malcolm X
entries.subtitle: Black nationalist leader and critic of nonviolence

cards.a: Black nationalist leader and critic of nonviolence. Minister and national spokesman, Nation of Islam; Founder, Organization of Afro-American Unity (1964)
Born May 19, 1925, Omaha, Nebraska; died February 21, 1965, New York City

cards.q: Who is this? Black nationalist leader and critic of nonviolence
cards.a: Malcolm X
May 19, 1925, Omaha, Nebraska, as Malcolm Little
Joined in prison; minister after his 1952 release; national spokesman by the late 1950s
Left the Nation of Islam in spring 1964; pilgrimage to Mecca
Once, at the U.S. Capitol, March 1964
Malcolm X gave voice to Black anger and pride and offered a radical alternative to King’s philosophy, and his influence grew after his death.

cards.q: What shaped Malcolm X early in life?
cards.a: Malcolm Little was born on May 19, 1925, in Omaha, Nebraska. His parents were active in Marcus Garvey’s movement — his father led a chapter of the Universal Negro Improvement Association — and his father’s activism drew threats from a white supremacist group, the Black Legion.

cards.q: What were Malcolm X’s major achievements?
cards.a: Brilliant and charismatic, Malcolm X became a minister and national spokesman of the Nation of Islam, founding mosques in cities such as Detroit and Harlem and using newspaper columns, radio, and television to spread its message.

entries.title: Manifest Destiny
entries.subtitle: The belief that the United States was destined to spread across the continent

cards.a: The belief that the United States was destined to spread across the continent

cards.q: Name it: The belief that the United States was destined to spread across the continent
cards.a: Manifest Destiny
1845, by John O’Sullivan, in “Annexation,” The United States Magazine and Democratic Review
A destiny “to overspread the continent allotted by Providence”
President James K. Polk and the Democratic Party

Manifest Destiny gave a confident, providential name to the conquest of the continent. Historians today use it to examine how ideals of freedom and expansion were joined to dispossession and racial hierarchy.

Manifest Destiny combined three beliefs: that the United States had a special mission to spread democracy and freedom; that this mission was ordained by God (“Providence”); and that it was obvious — “manifest” — and therefore inevitable.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: O’Sullivan wrote in 1845 to urge the annexation of Texas, which he argued Britain and France were trying to block.

entries.title: Manzanar
entries.subtitle: A War Relocation Center in California’s Owens Valley, now a National Historic Site

cards.a: A War Relocation Center in California’s Owens Valley, now a National Historic Site
Owens Valley, Inyo County, California (between Lone Pine and Independence on U.S. 395) · West

cards.q: Name it: A War Relocation Center in California’s Owens Valley, now a National Historic Site
cards.a: Manzanar
Spanish for “apple orchard”
1942, on 6,200 acres leased by the Army from Los Angeles
About 800 during the war; all but three were dismantled or moved afterward
Held each year on the last Saturday of April, sponsored by the Manzanar Committee
Manzanar National Historic Site, National Park Service
Manzanar’s layered history of removal — Paiute, settler, and Japanese American — makes it a powerful place to reflect on who has been forced from the land.

Manzanar lies on the floor of the Owens Valley, with Mount Williamson rising directly to the west. Most of the camp’s buildings are gone; the site includes a cemetery, historic orchards, and a visitor center.

Earlier displacements. People used the Owens Valley for almost 10,000 years, and about 1,500 years ago the Owens Valley Paiute established settlements there, practicing a form of irrigated agriculture. After miners and ranchers moved in during the 1860s, the Army forcibly relocated nearly 1,000 Paiute to Fort Tejon in 1863.

entries.title: Mark Twain
entries.subtitle: Humorist and novelist who turned American speech into literature

cards.a: Humorist and novelist who turned American speech into literature. Riverboat pilot; Journalist and travel writer; Novelist and humorist; Lecturer; Vice president of the Anti-Imperialist League (1901–1910)
Born November 30, 1835, Florida, Missouri; died April 21, 1910, Redding, Connecticut

cards.q: Who is this? Humorist and novelist who turned American speech into literature
cards.a: Mark Twain
“Mark Twain,” a riverboat term — first used while writing for a Nevada newspaper
Hannibal, Missouri, on the Mississippi River
The Innocents Abroad (1869), Tom Sawyer (1876), Life on the Mississippi (1883), Huckleberry Finn (1884)
Anti-imperialist; vice president of the Anti-Imperialist League, 1901–1910

Mark Twain gave American literature its own voice — vernacular, funny, and morally serious — and his books remain central to how Americans imagine the nineteenth century, including its racism and its greed.

cards.q: What shaped Mark Twain early in life?
cards.a: Samuel Clemens was born on November 30, 1835, in Florida, Missouri, the sixth of seven children, and at four moved with his family to Hannibal, a small frontier town on the Mississippi River.

cards.q: What were Mark Twain’s major achievements?
cards.a: His comic story about a jumping frog, reprinted in papers across the country in 1865, was his first big break. Sent to report from the Sandwich Islands (Hawaii) in 1866, he came back and launched a career as a stage lecturer.

entries.title: Martin Luther King Jr.
entries.subtitle: Minister and leader of the nonviolent civil rights movement

cards.q: Who was Martin Luther King Jr.?
cards.a: Minister and leader of the nonviolent civil rights movement. Pastor, Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, Montgomery (from 1954); President, Montgomery Improvement Association (1955); President, Southern Christian Leadership Conference (from 1957); Co-pastor, Ebenezer Baptist Church, Atlanta (from 1960); Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1964)

cards.q: When did Martin Luther King Jr. live?
cards.a: Born January 15, 1929, Atlanta, Georgia; died April 4, 1968, Memphis, Tennessee

cards.q: Who is this? Minister and leader of the nonviolent civil rights movement
cards.a: Martin Luther King Jr.
January 15, 1929, Atlanta, Georgia, as Michael Luther King Jr.
Morehouse College (B.A. 1948); Crozer Theological Seminary (B.D. 1951); Boston University (Ph.D. 1955)
Married Coretta Scott in 1953; four children
Between 1957 and 1968 he traveled more than six million miles, spoke more than 2,500 times, and was arrested upwards of twenty times
1964, at age 35; he gave the prize money to the civil rights movement
April 4, 1968, at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, Tennessee

cards.q: Why does Martin Luther King Jr. matter?
cards.a: King gave the civil rights movement its moral voice and showed how nonviolent mass protest could change American law and conscience. In his last years he pressed the nation to confront poverty and war as well as segregation.

cards.q: What shaped Martin Luther King Jr. early in life?
cards.a: King was born in Atlanta on January 15, 1929, as Michael Luther King Jr.; his name was later changed to Martin. Preaching ran in the family.

cards.q: What were Martin Luther King Jr.’s major achievements?
cards.a: King was still new to Montgomery when Rosa Parks was arrested on December 1, 1955. On December 5, Black leaders formed the Montgomery Improvement Association and elected him president.

entries.title: Muhammad Ali
entries.subtitle: Three-time heavyweight champion who gave up his title rather than fight in Vietnam

cards.a: Three-time heavyweight champion who gave up his title rather than fight in Vietnam. Olympic gold medalist (Rome, 1960); Three-time world heavyweight champion; Conscientious objector to the Vietnam War; United Nations Messenger of Peace (2002)
Born January 17, 1942, Louisville, Kentucky; died June 2016

cards.q: Who is this? Three-time heavyweight champion who gave up his title rather than fight in Vietnam
cards.a: Muhammad Ali
Light heavyweight, Rome, 1960, at age eighteen
Beat Sonny Liston in Miami on February 25, 1964
Refused induction into the Army in 1967; stripped of his title and convicted
Clay v. United States (1971) unanimously reversed his conviction
Lost to Joe Frazier (1971); beat George Foreman in Zaire, the “Rumble in the Jungle” (1974)
Lit the cauldron at the 1996 Atlanta Games

Ali joined a champion’s boxing career to the politics of the civil rights movement and opposition to the Vietnam War. By sacrificing his title for his beliefs, he showed that an athlete could take a public stand — and inspired others, including the athletes who protested at the 1968 Olympics.

cards.q: What shaped Muhammad Ali early in life?
cards.a: Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. was born on January 17, 1942, in Louisville, Kentucky, and grew up with his parents, Odessa and Cassius Clay Sr., and his brother, Rudolph, in a house at 3302 Grand Avenue in the city’s West End. He attended mostly Black public schools.

cards.q: What were Muhammad Ali’s major achievements?
cards.a: On February 25, 1964, in Miami, the young challenger knocked out Sonny Liston in the seventh round to become heavyweight champion of the world. Just before the fight he publicly announced his conversion to the Nation of Islam, and he declared: “Cassius Clay is a slave name.

entries.title: Neil Armstrong
entries.subtitle: Test pilot and astronaut who became the first person to walk on the Moon, on July 20, 1969

cards.a: Test pilot and astronaut who became the first person to walk on the Moon, on July 20, 1969. Navy pilot in the Korean War; NACA/NASA research test pilot (1955–1962); NASA astronaut (selected 1962); Commander of Apollo 11; Professor of engineering, University of Cincinnati (1971–1979)
Born August 5, 1930, Wapakoneta, Ohio; died August 25, 2012

cards.q: Who is this? Test pilot and astronaut who became the first person to walk on the Moon, on July 20, 1969
cards.a: Neil Armstrong
78 combat missions as a Navy jet pilot
Seven flights, 1960–1962; top speed 3,989 mph (Mach 5.74)
March 16, 1966: first docking of two spacecraft in orbit
First person on the Moon, July 20, 1969
August 25, 2012, aged 82

Armstrong’s first step on the Moon was the climax of the Space Race and fulfilled the national goal set by President John F. Kennedy. His career as a pilot and engineer, from the X-15 to the Moon, spanned the leap from the jet age to the space age.

cards.q: What shaped Neil Armstrong early in life?
cards.a: Armstrong was born on August 5, 1930, in Wapakoneta, Ohio, and was drawn to flight and engineering.

cards.q: What were Neil Armstrong’s major achievements?
cards.a: In 1955 Armstrong joined the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA), NASA’s predecessor, and became a research test pilot at its flight station at Edwards, California.

entries.title: Republicanism
entries.subtitle: The founders’ ideal of self-government by virtuous citizens

cards.a: The founders’ ideal of self-government by virtuous citizens

cards.q: Name it: The founders’ ideal of self-government by virtuous citizens
cards.a: Republicanism
Liberty as freedom from arbitrary power, protected by self-government under law
Cicero and Roman historians, Machiavelli, the English republicans, Montesquieu, the eighteenth-century “commonwealthmen”
The Republican Party, founded in 1854

Republicanism gave Americans the language they used to justify independence and design their governments. Its insistence that liberty means freedom from domination also gave later reformers — abolitionists, labor activists, suffragists — a vocabulary for challenging the exclusions the founding generation left in place.
Political philosophers use “republicanism” in two related senses.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: Revolutionary Americans drew on this tradition to interpret British policy.

entries.title: Richard Nixon
entries.subtitle: Thirty-seventh president: opened relations with China, then became the only president to resign

cards.a: Thirty-seventh president: opened relations with China, then became the only president to resign. U.S. Representative from California (1947–1950); U.S. Senator from California (1950–1953); Vice president under Eisenhower (1953–1961); Thirty-seventh president (1969–1974)
Born January 9, 1913, Yorba Linda, California; died April 22, 1994

cards.q: Who is this? Thirty-seventh president: opened relations with China, then became the only president to resign
cards.a: Richard Nixon
January 20, 1969 – August 9, 1974; Republican
Visited Beijing in February 1972 — “Only Nixon could go to China”
First president to visit Moscow; signed the SALT and Anti-Ballistic Missile treaties in 1972
Won 49 of 50 states, all but Massachusetts
Signed laws creating OSHA (1970) and the Endangered Species Act (1973); proposed the EPA
August 9, 1974, facing impeachment; pardoned by Gerald Ford a month later

Nixon's diplomacy with China and the Soviet Union reshaped the Cold War and set the stage for its end, and his presidency marked the shift from liberal Democratic to conservative Republican dominance. Watergate made him a lasting symbol of the abuse of presidential power and deepened Americans' distrust of their leaders.

cards.q: What shaped Richard Nixon early in life?
cards.a: Nixon was born on January 9, 1913, in Yorba Linda, California, and grew up in another small town, East Whittier. His father, Frank, was argumentative, his mother, Hannah, sweet-tempered.

cards.q: What were Richard Nixon’s major achievements?
cards.a: In 1952 Dwight Eisenhower chose Nixon as his running mate. When a newspaper charged that a secret fund kept him in style, he defended himself on national television, promising his little daughter Tricia that he would never return one campaign gift — a cocker spaniel puppy named Checkers.

entries.title: Ronald Reagan
entries.subtitle: Fortieth president and leader of the conservative revival

cards.a: Fortieth president and leader of the conservative revival. Radio sports announcer; Film actor (1937–1957) and president of the Screen Actors Guild; Host of General Electric Theater; Governor of California (1967–1975); Fortieth president (1981–1989)
Born February 6, 1911, Tampico, Illinois; died June 5, 2004

cards.q: Who is this? Fortieth president and leader of the conservative revival
cards.a: Ronald Reagan
February 6, 1911, Tampico, Illinois; grew up in Dixon, Illinois
Sports announcer; about fifty films (1937–1957); president of the Screen Actors Guild; host of General Electric Theater
Governor of California, elected 1966 and reelected 1970
1980: defeated Carter, 489 electoral votes to 49; 1984: defeated Mondale, 525 to 13, carrying 49 states
Large income-tax cuts (1981), Tax Reform Act (1986); top marginal rate cut from 70 to 28 percent
Four summits with Gorbachev; INF Treaty signed December 1987

Reagan made conservatism, with its calls for lower taxes, less regulation, a strong military, and firm anticommunism, the dominant force in the Republican Party and a powerful one in American politics. His partnership with Gorbachev helped bring the Cold War toward a peaceful end, while his economic record, with long growth, low inflation, and record deficits, is still debated.

cards.q: What shaped Ronald Reagan early in life?
cards.a: Ronald Wilson Reagan was born on February 6, 1911, in an apartment above a general store in Tampico, Illinois.

cards.q: What were Ronald Reagan’s major achievements?
cards.a: A Time for Choosing. On October 27, 1964, Reagan gave a nationally televised speech for the Republican presidential candidate Barry Goldwater. He warned that government was eroding individual freedom and that the country was too weak against the Soviet Union, and told viewers, “You and I have a rendezvous with destiny.”

entries.title: Rosa Parks
entries.subtitle: Activist whose arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott

cards.a: Activist whose arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott. Secretary of the Montgomery NAACP (1943–1956); Adviser to the NAACP Youth Council; Dispatcher for the Montgomery Improvement Association carpool; Office assistant to Rep. John Conyers (until 1988)
Born February 4, 1913, Tuskegee, Alabama; died October 24, 2005

cards.q: Who is this? Activist whose arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott
cards.a: Rosa Parks
Joined the Montgomery branch in 1943 and served as its secretary until 1956
December 1, 1955, charged with “refusing to obey orders of bus driver”
381 or 382 days, December 1955 to December 1956, by about 17,000 Black residents
Moved to Detroit in 1957; worked for Rep. John Conyers until 1988
Congressional Gold Medal (1999); lay in honor in the U.S. Capitol (2005)

Parks’s refusal became the most famous single act of the civil rights movement, but its power came from years of organizing behind it. Her arrest gave Montgomery’s Black community the rallying point it had been looking for, and the boycott that followed showed that nonviolent mass protest could defeat segregation.

cards.q: What shaped Rosa Parks early in life?
cards.a: Rosa Louise McCauley was born on February 4, 1913, in Tuskegee, Alabama, and spent her first years on a small farm with her mother, grandparents, and brother. As a child she watched the Ku Klux Klan ride at night and listened in fear to news of lynchings near her home. She grew up in Montgomery, attended an industrial school for girls and the laboratory school of Alabama State College, and later enrolled at Alabama State Teachers College, but had to withdraw when her grandmother fell ill.

cards.q: What were Rosa Parks’s major achievements?
cards.a: On the evening of December 1, 1955, Parks, then forty-two, boarded a city bus on her way home from the Montgomery Fair department store, where she worked as a seamstress. Montgomery reserved the front ten seats of each bus for white passengers, and Parks sat in the first row behind them.

entries.title: Sacagawea
entries.subtitle: The Lemhi Shoshone teenager who traveled with Lewis and Clark’s Corps of Discovery

cards.a: The Lemhi Shoshone teenager who traveled with Lewis and Clark’s Corps of Discovery. Member of the Corps of Discovery (1805–1806); Interpreter and intermediary
Born c. 1788, Lemhi County, Idaho; died c. 1812, Fort Manuel Lisa

cards.q: Who is this? The Lemhi Shoshone teenager who traveled with Lewis and Clark’s Corps of Discovery
cards.a: Sacagawea
Lemhi Shoshone, from present-day Idaho
At about eleven or twelve, by a Hidatsa raiding party
Left the Mandan and Hidatsa villages in April 1805 with her two-month-old son
The only woman in the expedition; interpreter with her husband, Toussaint Charbonneau
“A woman with a party of men is a token of peace”

Sacagawea is one of the most commemorated women in American history and a reminder that the expedition depended on Native people. Her real story — a captive teenager and young mother whose presence and knowledge helped the Corps survive — is both more modest and more remarkable than the legend of the guide who led the way west.

cards.q: What shaped Sacagawea early in life?
cards.a: Sacagawea was born around 1788 among the Lemhi Shoshone in the mountains of present-day Idaho. When she was about eleven or twelve, a Hidatsa raiding party captured her and carried her east to the Hidatsa villages on the Knife River in present-day North Dakota, where she lived at the Awatixa village.

Meriwether Lewis and William Clark met her at the Mandan and Hidatsa villages in 1804 and hired Charbonneau as an interpreter; Sacagawea came too, valued for her knowledge of the tribes and terrain farther west.

entries.title: Sitting Bull
entries.subtitle: Hunkpapa Lakota leader who refused the reservation

cards.a: Hunkpapa Lakota leader who refused the reservation. Hunkpapa Lakota war leader; Leader of the Strong Heart warrior society; Spiritual leader; Leader of the non-treaty Lakota; Performer in Buffalo Bill’s Wild West (1885)
Born c. 1831, Near the Grand and Missouri Rivers, present-day South Dakota; died December 15, 1890, Standing Rock Reservation

cards.q: Who is this? Hunkpapa Lakota leader who refused the reservation
cards.a: Sitting Bull
Between 1831 and 1837, near the confluence of the Grand and Missouri Rivers, present-day South Dakota
Hunkpapa band of the Lakota
Refused to take part; became leader of the non-treaty Lakota
June 25–26, 1876; his village was attacked by Custer’s 7th Cavalry, which lost five companies under Custer
Led followers to Canada in 1877; surrendered at Fort Buford, July 20, 1881
December 15, 1890, killed during an arrest at his cabin on the Standing Rock Reservation

Sitting Bull became the best-known symbol of Native resistance to American conquest of the Great Plains. His refusal to sign away Lakota land or way of life, and the victory at the Little Bighorn associated with his name, made him famous among white Americans as well as his own people.

cards.q: What shaped Sitting Bull early in life?
cards.a: Sitting Bull was born into a prominent Hunkpapa Lakota family sometime between 1831 and 1837, near where the Grand River meets the Missouri in present-day South Dakota.

cards.q: What were Sitting Bull’s major achievements?
cards.a: The non-treaty Lakota. In 1866 the Lakota leader Red Cloud waged a successful war against forts along the Bozeman Trail, and in 1868 he and other leaders signed the Treaty of Fort Laramie.

entries.title: Slavery in America
entries.subtitle: The institution that shaped the nation’s economy, politics, and conflicts for nearly 250 years

cards.a: The institution that shaped the nation’s economy, politics, and conflicts for nearly 250 years

cards.q: Name it: The institution that shaped the nation’s economy, politics, and conflicts for nearly 250 years
cards.a: Slavery in America

cards.q: Africans forced onto the Middle Passage
cards.a: About 12.5 million, 1517–1867, to all of the Americas; about 10.7 million survived
cards.l: Africans forced onto the Middle Passage

cards.a: About 388,000 (the American Yawp estimates about 450,000), a small share of the total trade
654,121 in the South in 1790; 3,953,760 nationwide in 1860, about 12.6 percent of Americans
About 1 in 5 families in slave states; 49 percent in Mississippi and 46 percent in South Carolina
More than 1 million people moved from the Upper South to the Deep South, 1790–1860
Thirteenth Amendment, ratified December 6, 1865

cards.q: Why does Slavery in America matter?
cards.a: Slavery was not a regional exception to American history but one of its central forces.
Chattel slavery treated enslaved people as movable property that could be bought, sold, mortgaged, and inherited. In the English colonies and the United States, it became tied to race.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: Origins. Slavery in the Americas grew out of a much older Atlantic trade.

entries.title: Sojourner Truth
entries.subtitle: Abolitionist and women’s rights speaker who escaped slavery in New York

cards.a: Abolitionist and women’s rights speaker who escaped slavery in New York. Abolitionist and women’s rights lecturer; Preacher; Recruiter for Black Union troops; Freedmen’s relief worker
Born c. 1797, Ulster County, New York; died November 26, 1883, Battle Creek, Michigan

cards.q: Who is this? Abolitionist and women’s rights speaker who escaped slavery in New York
cards.a: Sojourner Truth
About 1797, enslaved in Ulster County, New York; she spoke only Dutch as a child
Escaped with her infant daughter in 1826
Sued to recover her son Peter, illegally sold to Alabama, and won
Took the name Sojourner Truth in 1843
Sojourner Truth made the case, from her own experience, that the struggles against slavery and for women’s rights were one struggle — and that neither could succeed while ignoring Black women.

cards.q: What shaped Sojourner Truth early in life?
cards.a: Isabella Baumfree was born about 1797 in Ulster County, New York, one of perhaps ten to twelve children of enslaved parents, James and Elizabeth; all her siblings were sold away. Her first language was the Dutch of her enslavers.

cards.q: What were Sojourner Truth’s major achievements?
cards.a: When Dumont illegally sold her five-year-old son Peter to an enslaver in Alabama, she took the case to court and, after a long fight, won his return in 1828 — becoming, the National Women’s History Museum notes, the first Black woman to sue a white man and win. A religious awakening followed.

entries.title: Susan B. Anthony
entries.subtitle: Organizer and public face of the woman suffrage movement

cards.a: Organizer and public face of the woman suffrage movement. Teacher; Temperance and antislavery reformer; American Anti-Slavery Society agent; Co-founder of the National Woman Suffrage Association (1869); Publisher of *The Revolution*; President of the National American Woman Suffrage Association (1892–1900)

cards.q: When did Susan B. Anthony live?
cards.a: Born February 15, 1820, Adams, Massachusetts; died March 13, 1906, Rochester, New York

cards.q: Who is this? Organizer and public face of the woman suffrage movement
cards.a: Susan B. Anthony
February 15, 1820, Adams, Massachusetts, the second of seven children
Met Elizabeth Cady Stanton in 1851; they worked together for the rest of their lives
Published from 1868; motto “Men, their rights, and nothing more; women, their rights, and nothing less”
Voted in the 1872 presidential election; arrested November 18, 1872; convicted and fined $100 in June 1873
National Woman Suffrage Association (1869); president of the National American Woman Suffrage Association, 1892–1900
March 13, 1906, Rochester, New York; buried in Mount Hope Cemetery

cards.q: Why does Susan B. Anthony matter?
cards.a: Anthony turned woman suffrage into a national, organized movement and kept it focused on a federal constitutional amendment. Her record also includes the racist arguments she adopted after the Civil War, which divided the movement and alienated former allies such as Frederick Douglass.

cards.q: What shaped Susan B. Anthony early in life?
cards.a: Susan Brownell Anthony was born on February 15, 1820, in Adams, Massachusetts, the second of seven children of Daniel and Lucy Anthony. Her father, a Quaker, built a cotton mill, where Susan worked for a time with one of her sisters.

cards.q: What were Susan B. Anthony’s major achievements?
cards.a: Partnership with Stanton. In 1851, on a street corner in Seneca Falls, Amelia Bloomer introduced Anthony to Elizabeth Cady Stanton, the organizer of the 1848 Seneca Falls convention. Their partnership lasted the rest of their lives.

entries.title: Tecumseh
entries.subtitle: Shawnee leader who built a confederacy of Native nations

cards.a: Shawnee leader who built a confederacy of Native nations. Shawnee war leader and diplomat; Organizer of a pan-Native confederacy; British ally in the War of 1812
Born c. 1768, Scioto River valley, present-day Ohio; died October 5, 1813, Near Moraviantown, Upper Canada (Ontario)

cards.q: Who is this? Shawnee leader who built a confederacy of Native nations
cards.a: Tecumseh
About 1768, in the Ohio country
Tenskwatawa, a religious leader known as “the Prophet”
Prophetstown, at the junction of the Wabash and Tippecanoe Rivers, Indiana
October 5, 1813, at the Battle of the Thames

Tecumseh offered the most ambitious Native answer to American expansion: a confederacy of nations defending their land in common. Its defeat opened the Midwest and South to rapid settlement and Indian removal.

cards.q: What shaped Tecumseh early in life?
cards.a: Tecumseh was born about 1768 in a Kispoko Shawnee village in the Scioto River valley of present-day Ohio, the son of Pukeshinwau, of the Panther Clan, and Methoataaskee, of the Turtle Clan. His parents had family ties to the Shawnee communities living among the Creeks in present-day Alabama — connections he would later draw on.

In the early 1800s, Tecumseh’s brother Tenskwatawa began preaching a spiritual revival that called on Native people to reject American goods and customs and return to their own ways. The brothers founded a village, Prophetstown, in Indiana, which drew followers from many nations.

entries.title: The Blues
entries.subtitle: The African American music of the Deep South that became the root of jazz, rock and roll, and soul

cards.a: The African American music of the Deep South that became the root of jazz, rock and roll, and soul

cards.q: Name it: The African American music of the Deep South that became the root of jazz, rock and roll, and soul
cards.a: The Blues
Probably in the 1880s or 1890s, in the Deep South
Usually twelve bars, using three basic chords and flattened “blue notes”
W. C. Handy heard a guitarist play with a knife for a slide at Tutwiler, Mississippi, around 1903
No African American recorded the blues until 1920; women vaudeville singers dominated 1920–1925
Charley Patton, Son House, Robert Johnson, Muddy Waters, Howlin’ Wolf, B. B. King

The blues documented the experience of Black Southerners more fully than perhaps any other form of expression, and its forms, sounds, and spirit fed directly into jazz, rhythm and blues, rock and roll, and soul — making it one of the most influential musical traditions in the world.

Musically, the blues is typified by a twelve-bar chord progression — each verse stretches over twelve measures using set patterns of three basic chords — although other lengths are common. Its signature is the “blue note,” a flattened third, fifth, or seventh that gives the music its aching sound.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: The blues grew out of the music that enslaved Africans and their descendants made in the South: work songs and field hollers sung in the fields, and the spirituals of Black churches. It appeared in recognizable form in the 1880s or 1890s, and by the early 1900s it was spreading across the South from Virginia to Texas.

entries.title: The Columbian Exchange
entries.subtitle: The transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between the hemispheres after 1492

cards.a: The transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between the hemispheres after 1492

cards.q: Name it: The transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between the hemispheres after 1492
cards.a: The Columbian Exchange
Maize, white and sweet potatoes, manioc, peanuts, tomatoes, squash, pineapples, avocados
Wheat, rice, barley, sugar, horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, goats
Smallpox, measles, malaria, yellow fever, typhoid, and others
Alfred W. Crosby, in his 1972 book The Columbian Exchange

cards.q: Why does the Columbian Exchange matter?
cards.a: The Columbian Exchange reshaped ecosystems, diets, and populations on every inhabited continent. For the Americas it meant both the arrival of new livestock and crops and the greatest population collapse in human history — a central reason why European colonization succeeded.

The Columbian Exchange is the movement of living things — plants, animals, and pathogens — and of people between the Old World and the New after Columbus’s voyages reconnected hemispheres that had developed separately for thousands of years.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: Before 1492, the Americas and the Eastern Hemisphere had very different inventories of life. The Americas had few domesticated animals — dogs, llamas, guinea pigs, and a few fowl — and no wild horses or cattle to tame.

entries.title: The Digital Revolution
entries.subtitle: Computers, the internet, and smartphones transform American life

cards.a: Computers, the internet, and smartphones transform American life
1969–present

cards.q: Name it: Computers, the internet, and smartphones transform American life
cards.a: The Digital Revolution
Began with four computer nodes in late 1969
Launched 1986; grew from about 2,000 connected computers to more than 2 million by 1993
First freely available web browser, developed with NSF support at the University of Illinois
NSF retired the NSFNET backbone in 1995 as commercial services took over
The iPhone (2007) popularized smartphones; about two-thirds of Americans owned one by about 2015

cards.q: Why does the Digital Revolution matter?
cards.a: The digital revolution remade how Americans work, shop, learn, communicate, and get their news — and created new questions about privacy, misinformation, and economic inequality.

The term describes the shift, beginning in the late twentieth century, from industrial and analog technologies to digital computing and communications — and the economic, social, and political changes that followed.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: In the early 1960s J. C. R. Licklider imagined an “Intergalactic Computer Network.” Defense Department researchers built ARPANET and developed the TCP/IP protocols that let computers exchange email and files.

entries.title: The Gilded Age
entries.subtitle: An era of industrial wealth, inequality, and corruption, c. 1870–1900

cards.a: An era of industrial wealth, inequality, and corruption, c. 1870–1900

cards.q: Name it: An era of industrial wealth, inequality, and corruption, c. 1870–1900
cards.a: The Gilded Age
From The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today (1873) by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner
Andrew Carnegie, John D. Rockefeller, J. P. Morgan, Thomas Edison
By 1900, about 190,000 miles of railroad; Chicago grew from about 30,000 people in 1850 to 300,000 by 1870
Labor unions, Populism, and later Progressivism

cards.q: Why does the Gilded Age matter?
cards.a: The Gilded Age created modern industrial America — and the inequalities and conflicts that reformers in the Populist and Progressive movements set out to address.

A gilded object is covered with a thin layer of gold over a cheaper material. By calling their era “gilded” rather than golden, Twain and Warner mocked a society whose dazzling wealth and technological marvels masked massive social inequities and deep-seated corruption.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: After the Civil War, industrial capitalism transformed the country. The transcontinental railroad and a vast rail network created national markets.

entries.title: The National Mall
entries.subtitle: “America’s Front Yard” in Washington, D.C.

cards.a: “America’s Front Yard” in Washington, D.C.
Washington, D.C., from the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River · Washington, D.C.

cards.q: Name it: “America’s Front Yard” in Washington, D.C.
cards.a: The National Mall
From the foot of the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River
Pierre L’Enfant’s plan for the Federal City, commissioned by President George Washington (1791)
National Mall and Memorial Parks, National Park Service — more than 1,000 acres
Washington Monument; Lincoln, Jefferson, FDR, World War II, Korean War Veterans, Vietnam Veterans, and Martin Luther King Jr. memorials
24 hours a day

cards.q: Why does the National Mall matter?
cards.a: The National Park Service calls the Mall the premier civic and symbolic space in the nation — the place where Americans gather to remember, celebrate, and protest.
The Mall is a long swath of green lined with monuments and memorials.

The Mall’s open spaces date to L’Enfant’s plan for the original 1791 Federal City. Over two centuries, memorials were added to honor presidents, wars, and leaders; the Lincoln Memorial’s inscription declares that “the memory of Abraham Lincoln is enshrined forever.”

entries.title: The Underground Railroad
entries.subtitle: The secret network of freedom seekers and those who helped them escape slavery

cards.a: The secret network of freedom seekers and those who helped them escape slavery

cards.q: Name it: The secret network of freedom seekers and those who helped them escape slavery
cards.a: The Underground Railroad
Escape from slavery through flight, and assistance with that escape, from slavery’s beginning to the Civil War
The free states, Canada, Mexico, Spanish Florida, Indian Territory, the West, the Caribbean, and Europe
Harriet Tubman: “I never ran my train off the track and I never lost a passenger”
The Fugitive Slave Act paid federal commissioners $10 if they ruled a captive enslaved but only $5 if free
The Black abolitionist William Still helped freedom seekers and preserved their letters and stories

cards.q: Why does the Underground Railroad matter?
cards.a: The Underground Railroad was one of the earliest grassroots movements in American history in which people united across lines of race, gender, religion, and class to defy unjust laws.
The goal was freedom. Enslaved people sought to escape bondage and reach places where they could live free and beyond the reach of recapture.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: Escape began at the place of enslavement. Freedom seekers followed rivers, canals, bays, the Atlantic coast, roads, and trails, and drew on courage and ingenuity — disguises, forgeries, and other strategies — to evade slave catchers who watched the expected routes for rewards.

entries.title: Theodore Roosevelt
entries.subtitle: Twenty-sixth president and champion of the “Square Deal”

cards.a: Twenty-sixth president and champion of the “Square Deal”. New York assemblyman (1882–1884); U.S. Civil Service commissioner; President of the New York City Police Board; Assistant secretary of the Navy (1897–1898); Rough Rider in the Spanish-American War; Governor of New York; Vice president (1901); Twenty-sixth president (1901–1909); Progressive (“Bull Moose”) Party candidate (1912)
Born October 27, 1858, New York City; died January 6, 1919, Oyster Bay, New York

cards.q: Who is this? Twenty-sixth president and champion of the “Square Deal”
cards.a: Theodore Roosevelt
1901–1909; Republican; took office after McKinley’s assassination and was elected in his own right in 1904
The Square Deal: the Northern Securities suit, the Hepburn Act, the Meat Inspection and Pure Food and Drug Acts (1906)
150 national forests, 51 bird reserves, 5 national parks, and 18 national monuments
“Speak softly and carry a big stick”; Panama Canal; Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine
For mediating the end of the Russo-Japanese War (1905); the first U.S. president to win it
Roosevelt changed what Americans expected of a president.

cards.q: What shaped Theodore Roosevelt early in life?
cards.a: Theodore Roosevelt was born in New York City on October 27, 1858, the second of four children of Theodore Roosevelt Sr., a wealthy businessman and philanthropist, and Martha “Mittie” Roosevelt, who had grown up on a Georgia plantation. A sickly child with asthma, “Teedie” resolved as a teenager to “make his body” through gymnastics and weight-lifting, and he remained a lifelong champion of exercise and what he called the “strenuous life.” He was taught at home, traveled with his family in Europe and the Middle East, and entered Harvard College in 1876, where he studied natural history and took up boxing and wrestling. In October 1880 he married Alice Hathaway Lee.

cards.q: What were Theodore Roosevelt’s major achievements?
cards.a: The Square Deal. Roosevelt believed government had the right to regulate big business for the public good, though he did not want to abolish it. In 1902 his Justice Department sued the Northern Securities Company, a giant railroad combination organized by J. P. Morgan and other financiers, under the Sherman Antitrust Act.

entries.title: Thomas Edison
entries.subtitle: Inventor of the phonograph and a practical electric light, and creator of the modern research laboratory

cards.a: Inventor of the phonograph and a practical electric light, and creator of the modern research laboratory. Telegrapher; Inventor; Industrialist; Head of the Naval Consulting Board (World War I)
Born February 11, 1847, Milan, Ohio; died October 18, 1931, West Orange, New Jersey

cards.q: Who is this? Inventor of the phonograph and a practical electric light, and creator of the modern research laboratory
cards.a: Thomas Edison
1877: the first machine that could record and play back sound
A carbonized-thread filament burned for 13½ hours; Menlo Park was lit up in December 1879
Pearl Street, lower Manhattan, opened in September 1882 — “the electric age had begun”
Menlo Park (1876), the first of its kind; West Orange (1887), where up to 10,000 people worked during World War I
A special Congressional medal in 1928

Edison did not just invent devices; he built complete systems — power plants, wiring, records, film studios — that turned inventions into industries, and his research laboratory became the model for modern corporate science. Electric light, recorded sound, and movies reshaped everyday American life.

cards.q: What shaped Thomas Edison early in life?
cards.a: Thomas Alva Edison was born on February 11, 1847, in Milan, Ohio, the seventh and last child of Samuel and Nancy Edison; when he was seven the family moved to Port Huron, Michigan. He attended school for only a few months.

cards.q: What were Thomas Edison’s major achievements?
cards.a: In 1876 Edison moved to the village of Menlo Park, New Jersey, and built a laboratory equipped to work on any invention — the first research and development lab anywhere, sometimes called his greatest invention.

entries.title: Thomas Jefferson
entries.subtitle: Author of the Declaration of Independence and third president

cards.a: Author of the Declaration of Independence and third president. Principal author of the Declaration of Independence; Governor of Virginia (1779–1781); Minister to France (1785–1789); First U.S. secretary of state; Vice president (1797–1801); Third president (1801–1809); Founder of the University of Virginia
Born April 13, 1743, Shadwell, Virginia; died July 4, 1826, Monticello, Virginia

cards.q: Who is this? Author of the Declaration of Independence and third president
cards.a: Thomas Jefferson
April 13, 1743 (April 2, Old Style), at Shadwell, Virginia
Republican (Democratic-Republican), which he founded with James Madison in the 1790s
Lost to John Adams in 1796 (71–68); tied with Aaron Burr in 1800 (73 each) and won in the House on the 36th ballot; reelected easily in 1804
1803: 828,000 square miles for $15 million, about four cents an acre
More than 600 over his lifetime, of whom he freed only a handful
